news:edition.news:latestLongForm: India has to export AI and robotics to grow at 8 to 9 percent
news:edition.news:briefing:
Sunday 22 November 2026, retrieved at 07:01 IST. Vani Kola says India has a little over 100 billion of fairly standard chip demand, at 28 and 65 nanometers, and should serve that market before it chases cutting-edge fabs. No currency is named for the 100 billion. Founders disagree on whether Sarvam can still be called sovereign while it hosts Chinese open-weight models. In Sanand, Kaynes Semicon says it intends to package close to 10 billion devices at full scale. That is a target, not current output. Subhashis Banerjee of Bharat1.ai says growth at 8 to 9 percent has to come from exporting AI and robotics.
The morning's through-line: Vani Kola says India should first serve a little over 100 billion of fairly standard chips, founders disagree on whether Sarvam stays sovereign while hosting Chinese open-weight models, and Kaynes Semicon intends to package close to 10 billion devices at full scale.
Standard chips. At the Bengaluru Tech Summit, Vani Kola, managing director of Kalaari Capital, says India should own its strengths rather than measure itself against Korea or China. She puts the home market at a little over 100 billion of fairly standard components. That is not cutting-edge GPUs. She says it is 28 and 65 nanometer chips, and that Tata Electronics and others are starting to produce them in India. These are not cutting-edge fabs. She says India already has the technology, the capability, and the manufacturing to serve its own demand first, and that global capability centres have given it the largest semiconductor talent pool in the world. She says India is not doing what she calls the 10 percent of cutting-edge research, design, development, and manufacturing. What that 10 percent measures is not explained. She says India should aspire to it as a later step. The written account calls her founder as well as managing director. The spoken introduction calls her a venture capitalist and managing director and does not say founder.
Exits. She says treating a stock-market listing as the only exit is a recurring mistake, and that making it the only outcome would crash the industry. Three companies exited significantly last year, and those were not listing stories. She does not name them. A couple of listings are coming in the next six to 12 months, also unnamed, and other exits are coming through acquisitions or secondary sales, which she treats as equally viable. The interviewer, not Kola, says the firm invested early in companies including Flipkart, had exits from Myntra, and that Cult.fit is about to list. She told Priyank Kharge this is the best edition of the summit she has attended. She says Bangalore still holds the centre of India's innovation economy. On AI, she compares it to electricity. India not having built the largest models, or the cutting-edge chips, is not a reason to stop inventing. Kalaari is looking at applications, embedded AI, and physical AI, including autonomy and vision.
Exports and physical AI. Subhashis Banerjee of Bharat1.ai says the first stage of building language models cost hundreds of billions of dollars and is mostly over. India could not join that stage because it does not have hundreds of billions of dollars. The title says India skipped the race. He says the next work is world models and physics-based models, and that India should build on the finished stack. The written account calls him co-founder and names the interviewer as Supreeth Koundinya. Neither is spoken.
He says the country wants to reach 30 trillion or 40 trillion, a figure he does not settle and does not give a currency for, and that there is no way to grow at 8 to 9 percent without exporting. The spoken line is "grow at 8 9%". The written account says 8 to 9 percent a year. He says no country has grown faster than the world without exporting, that a large part of India's growth over 25 years came from exporting IT services, and that a large part of remittances comes from Indian tech workers abroad. An older trillion-dollar company, he says, grew with 40,000 people, of whom he hoped 15,000 would come from India, plus a centre of another 30,000. Anthropic, which he says is about to list tomorrow or the day after, has only a three-digit headcount.
He says humanoid robots may look like a poor fit for India, where labour is cheaper than in the G7 and the population has not plateaued. Europe, Japan, South Korea, and the United States will need the machines, so Indian companies have to build them at home before they can sell them. In 10 to 15 years, he says, a very significant share of exports, and probably all of the increase over the next 10 years, will be AI and robotics. His example is food delivery. A Swiggy or Zomato order now goes from a kitchen by a delivery worker. Later, a building would take a coded delivery in the basement and move it by rail to the right person. He says physical AI can be learned only by doing it. He cites Addverb, which he says opened the world's largest robot factory in Noida about six or eight months earlier, and says 90 percent of its revenue comes from outside India. Companies that are only one API call, he says, will die when Anthropic ships a new feature. Predictions from two years earlier that all software companies would die have not come true, because large enterprises still run old systems, including COBOL. The line that "their growth has played" is unclear. Engineers are still needed. On talent, he says data he read about 78 days earlier, for July 2025 to June 2026 or a financial year he still needs to check, showed more people coming back to India than leaving. His own view is that job losses will probably slightly exceed new jobs. India cannot fund brute-force companies. It can build applications and physics-based AI.
Sarvam. Antara asks whether India is building its own AI or paying to run other companies' models. The written account names her Antara Gupta. The guests are Siddharth Panwar, chief executive of Mannas, also written as NeuroDx, Vishnu Ramesh of Asthra AI, and Vishnu Subramanian of JarvisLabs. Her question assumes that six of Sarvam's eight token-factory models are Chinese. The guests do not state that count. Vishnu Subramanian says banks and regulated firms cannot take intelligence from outside India, so models have to be hosted in the country. He says the best open-weight models in a period he calls "2022 26" come from China. He asks why American open weights would be acceptable if Chinese ones are the problem. He says Sarvam may serve the best open models while it builds better ones. He also says the government subsidized one Sarvam project, not the whole company. From news he has read, that project used 4,000 GPUs and is over. He then says they "raised like 300 billion dollars or something." Siddharth separately says a one-trillion-parameter model would probably cost 300 million dollars. Those are different claims.
Siddharth says hosting foreign models alone would not be sovereignty, but Sarvam also has its own models, so he would keep that word and argue only about whether it leads the world. For defence, he says, the government would ask Sarvam rather than a Chinese model or Mistral. He says subsidy recipients must open up their models, and that his own brain model is open. He says Mannas built what he calls the leading model under 1 billion parameters, and that training from scratch is not financially irresponsible. He says the government owns 1 to 2 percent of Sarvam. He has seen fraud allegations, in a word heard as "nonrupless," and he says he sees nothing wrong in the grant.
Vishnu Ramesh says a model he calls Sarvam 105B may have been slightly competitive. He has not seen it, and he expected it to slip against other models. He says extra products dilute the work. Sarvam has announced a coding agent and about five or six other things. His chief scientist, Professor Manish of IIIT Hyderabad, holds the team in high regard. Focus, he says, is what is missing. He would not stop because India trails DeepSeek or Google. Voice and Indian languages are the opening, and ElevenLabs is already being paid for that market. Antara says India is scaling to 58,000 subsidized GPUs. Vishnu Subramanian says that subsidized number is unknown. He puts the India figure at 10,000 crore and says the country did not spend billions of taxpayer dollars on Sarvam. Siddharth says a blocked Strait of Hormuz shook the economy, and that locked frontier intelligence would leave the country at someone else's mercy. The group does not settle whether India should build chips and foundation models or win the application layer.
Kaynes in Sanand. The account is a walk through the Kaynes Semicon plant. The written account says Sanjana Gupta tours it with Raghu Panicker, chief executive. The spoken account addresses Sanjana and does not say Raghu Panicker. The written account says six units. The spoken account itemizes units 1 through 6 and later says six or seven. The title's 10 billion devices is spoken as an intent, at full scale, to do close to 10 billion devices.
The site is given as 46 acres, about a kilometre from fence to fence. Customers supply the wafer. The route described runs from incoming inspection through wafer mount, wafer saw, die attach, curing, cleaning, aluminium and copper wire bonding, and tests named as a functional test, ball shear, die shear, and wire pull. A power module is said to hold 17 dice. Unit 2 is 16,000 square metres and still under construction, with about 480 to 485 manufacturing machines and a clean room of about 8,000 square metres. One plating line is running and a second is planned. The plating chemical is heard as citrine or citron and is said to come from Malaysia for now. A board-assembly area for communication modules is expected to run at the end of November. Power is 11 kilovolts now and is to become 66, with one line online and one standby. The water aim is zero liquid discharge. The yield he states as the standard is 99.999 percent. For a car-grade chip he says quality has to be 100 percent, because a chip in what is heard as an anti-breaking system has to open an airbag. The plant is IATF qualified. Later products are meant for two-wheelers and four-wheelers, then aerospace. Talks have started with the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad on sensors that must survive radiation and a wide temperature range. Headcount is 100, with a hope of 500 and 700 in three to four months, then thousands or 2,000 as unit 2 comes up. He says the Government of India has approved 12 companies and Kaynes is one. Micron and CG Semi are the other plants named in Sanand. He says the three do not compete with one another: memory, microcontrollers, and power modules he calls IPM 5 and IPM 7. He prefers Sanand because attrition is low compared with Bangalore.
Deriv. Deriv, an online trading firm with more than 26 years, more than 3 million traders, and 900 staff in 13 countries, released a staff platform called Deriv One under the MIT licence. The interviewer names the chief executive as Rakshit Choudhary. He asked for a list of AI skills. Staff returned 221 skills from 54 people, each described a little differently, and nobody could say who was allowed to run what. Ansh Choudhary says he remembers more than 400 skills later. Christopher Hernandez says a skill is a repeatable set of steps, the tools, the objective, and an optional structured result. An upload is checked for malicious commands and leaked secrets before it enters the registry. Access is decided by role. Client details an agent should not see are replaced with synthetic values. A Slack reply that others in the channel should not see is shown only to the person who asked. The interviewer says the target is to automate 75 percent of manual workflows by the end of this year. Neither guest gives a progress figure. Work started in May and was released about one or two months later. No year is given. Finance and compliance went first. The interviewer says five people built it. That count is not confirmed. Open-sourcing, Choudhary says, took about ten times the work, and some job candidates arrived having already changed the code. Hernandez says he would rather have the controls tested in public. The interviewer says the starter setup lets anyone who can reach it log in as an administrator, and that the default sandbox shares the host machine's kernel. Hernandez says the first change is to put in the organisation's own access rules. He does not name who should wait. He says companies should turn off autonomous assistants that are given too much access. Choudhary says an agent that can use a computer, and hand the work back when it is stuck, is the next addition within six months and already works inside Deriv.
After the token leaderboard. Rakesh Ravuri, chief technology officer of Publicis Sapient, says ranking staff by how much AI they use was a short-lived push to make people try the tools, not a plan to burn tokens. The introduction says that in April Meta ranked about 85,000 employees, gave first place the title token legend, and withdrew the table within a week, and that Microsoft had run a similar ranking since January. No year is attached to those months. By July the firm had a name for the habit: tokenmaxxing. A PwC survey of 4,454 chief executives, published in January, found 56 percent saying AI had brought no real significant financial benefit. Ravuri says the next scoreboard should show the value the tokens create. Leaders should put tokens on the work that pays back fastest and still fund experiments. He calls pure efficiency a faster caterpillar, not a butterfly. Meeting notes written by a model may be quicker. They do not change the process. He is taking apart a software life cycle used for 30 years. A team that had moved from a release every two weeks to one a week was told to ship three times a day, which forced a new line rather than a faster old one. The interviewer says a European bank in the firm's paper cut loan processing from 60 days to six. Ravuri talks about the 54 days left. The limit was time, not the money available to lend, and those days can go to choosing loans and collecting bad ones rather than to fewer staff. He will not say whether AI is paying for itself at Publicis Sapient. He calls that a forward-looking statement and says only that it has enough legs. If a finance chief wants the AI budget cut in half, he says he will find the money by creating value somewhere else. He expects the next empty contest to be pride in how many agents a person is running.
Karnataka. A minister for the state says the 2024 reservation bill, 50 percent of management jobs and 70 percent of non-management private jobs for locals, is paused, probably because of industry resistance. He says nobody will be hired only for being local. The wording of who must be made more employable is heard as "Canada," and the people of the state are heard as "Karnatikas." The title asks if the rule kills jobs. He does not say that. Speaking as IT minister, he calls data centres a necessary evil. He cannot refuse them, and he does not want a race to the bottom. He asks for better power utility effectiveness, water utility effectiveness, and newer technology, for the environment and the next generation. The title says data centres are becoming a major political issue. He does not say that.

news:edition.news:latestLongForm: TCS and Infosys opened higher as the AI trade fell
news:edition.news:briefing:
Saturday 21 November 2026, retrieved at 07:04 IST. Indian IT stocks rose on Friday morning while chipmakers and the wider AI trade fell. Anthropic priced a share sale of about 81.3 billion dollars at 83 dollars a share, and Reuters is cited for a valuation of about 1.5 trillion dollars. Google's Willow processor won a two-player coordination game 98.3 percent of the time, against a classical ceiling of 88.9 percent. Gemini 4 Neon is first on one coding-agent index with a score of 58.6, which is not a claim that it leads every coding test. GTA 6 is on sale for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, with no PC date. Priyank Kharge says Karnataka's Nipuna programme has promised five lakh jobs and has already started training close to 63,000 people.
The morning's through-line: Indian IT stocks rose as the AI trade fell, Anthropic's share sale is about 81.3 billion dollars at 83 dollars a share, and Karnataka's Nipuna programme has promised five lakh jobs with training already started for close to 63,000 people.
Indian IT. On Friday 20 November, just after the opening bell, the Nifty IT index was up more than 1 percent. TCS opened around 1.5 percent higher. Persistent Systems was among the IT stocks that gained, and the size of that gain was not finished. The written account also says Infosys opened higher. No separate Friday percentage was given for Infosys in the spoken account. There was no official reason, no large deal, and no results behind the move. Some of the buying is described as bargain hunting after a long decline this year. Infosys cut its growth forecast last month, and one strong morning does not repair that. This is not investment advice, and no buy call is made on TCS.
The same morning in reverse. On Thursday 19 November, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, made its stock-market debut and the shares closed about 17 percent above the listing price. Nvidia opened almost 5 percent higher, reversed, and closed more than 3 percent down. A shorter account says Nvidia flipped from a gain of 5 percent to a loss of 3 percent; the spoken line of that shorter account says "down three" and does not restate a percent. The Nasdaq gave up early gains and ended about 2.3 percent lower. By one Reuters count, Nvidia had lost around 2 trillion dollars from its October record by this week. The comparison offered for that loss is more than 1 lakh rupees for every person in India. In Tokyo, the Nikkei fell 4.5 percent in a single morning, and Asian markets were described as on track for their worst week since 2020. SoftBank, which has put about 64 billion dollars into OpenAI, had its worst day in more than two years and fell as much as 16 percent. On Thursday in Mumbai, the main indices rose while IT stocks slipped. Friday morning reversed that IT move.
February, and the opposite fear. About nine months before the listing, Anthropic released agents that could write code, test it, and run business software, work Indian IT companies are paid for. On one day the Nifty IT index fell almost 6 percent. That day is called the index's worst since 2020, and the spoken account calls it the steepest intraday fall since March 2020. Over that month TCS fell more than 15 percent. Infosys fell more than 20, and no unit is stated for that Infosys figure. This week's selling is described as a different fear. What was being sold were chipmakers, cloud companies, and investors who had bet on AI labs, the companies spending hundreds of billions of dollars on chips and data centers, as investors asked when that money comes back. TCS and Infosys do not make the chips and do not build those data centers. They sell people and services. If AI is slower and more expensive than promised, companies still need engineers. If it takes off, someone still has to put it into a bank, an airline, or a hospital. They do not win either way. This week they were not the ones holding the bill. In February, AI was expected to replace Indian IT. In November, when AI wobbled, Indian IT was where some investors went to hide. Whether that holds depends on what Wall Street does next.
Anthropic's books. The company offered 980 million shares at 83 dollars each. The title and the spoken account put that share sale at about 81.3 billion dollars and call it the world's largest initial public offering. A short written line calls 81.3 billion the valuation. The spoken account does not. It cites Reuters for an IPO valuation of about 1.5 trillion dollars. Shares traded above 110 dollars early on Nasdaq, more than 30 percent above the issue price. Most of the offering is newly issued shares. About 79.4 billion dollars in gross proceeds is attributable to Anthropic, the remainder goes to selling shareholders, and fees and expenses reduce what the company keeps. A separate 26 billion dollar private placement is planned alongside the offering and is subject to closing conditions. The rest of that condition was not stated. The public offering and the private placement are separate, and the headline amount is not entirely money flowing into Anthropic. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue was about 33.24 billion dollars and compute and infrastructure expenses were about 18.81 billion dollars. The written account gives an operating loss of 1.26 billion. The spoken line says about 1.26 and does not finish the unit. That operating loss is different from a larger reported net loss, which includes substantial non-cash financing charges. The net-loss figure is not given. Moneycontrol reported that platforms including one named IND money, and Groww, let people queue share orders before trading began. Those orders are subject to price limits and are not guaranteed allotments. Public reporting will make it easier to compare Anthropic's growth with the computing cost behind the revenue.
Willow. Google's Willow processor won a two-player game on a 3 by 3 grid 98.3 percent of the time. The classical ceiling is 88.9 percent, and the best classical strategy is described as eight wins out of nine. The players do not talk to each other. Each square is plus one or minus one, every row must multiply to plus one, every column must multiply to minus one, and they win if their answers match where the row and column meet. The hardware did not produce an impossible completed grid. It used quantum measurements to coordinate answers beyond a pre-arranged classical strategy. The account ties that to quantum contextuality: the outcomes are not all explained by assuming every property already carried a fixed answer, independent of which compatible measurements were made with it. A name heard as Sundar Pay, and later as Pichai, is credited with calling contextuality a possible deeper resource and with calling the result a sharper ruler for building better quantum systems. The spoken account also describes a multiplayer coordination game with up to 71 cubits, and a separate shallow-circuit run on up to 105 cubits. The written account says benchmarks on 105 qubits. The stated advantage is against classical circuits that are limited in how many sequential steps they can take. Together, the experiments are said to show quantum behavior still measurable on larger systems, and to expose subtle systematic hardware errors that conventional randomized benchmarks can miss. Chemistry and material science remain later ambitions. This result does not deliver them. The account places the result on Thursday, beside the GTA 6 launch.
Gemini 4 Neon. Google has introduced Gemini 4 Neon for software engineering, analytical work, and tasks that take several steps. The written spelling is Gemini 4 NEON. It is first on the artificial analysis coding agent index with a score of 58.6. That is a combined score, not a claim that Neon beats every competing model at coding. The index mixes understanding a codebase, changing code, fixing a bug, and work through a command line. A model can do well on one kind and struggle on another, and the testing organization advises reading the combined score next to the individual results. Google's published comparison shows Neon ahead on some evaluations, while Claude Opus 5.5 remains ahead on others, including Terminal Bench 4.1 and Frontier Code 2.0. Understanding an unfamiliar repository and successfully repairing it ask different things of an agent. Neon supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens, and Google lists documents, images, audio, and video among the inputs. It offers four thinking levels. API pricing is 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 dollars per million output tokens, with a lower rate for cached input and no figure given for that lower rate. The bill for a job depends on how many tokens are used, including extra attempts. Google is rolling Neon out through its developer and business services, with access for eligible paid users in a service named anti-gravity and in the Gemini app. Testing it on a team's own work will say more than one ranking.
GTA 6. Rockstar released GTA 6 on 19 November, 13 years after GTA 5, for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S. A PC release date has not been announced. A widely reported 1.1 billion dollar pre-order figure is Sensor Tower's estimate of sales through 10 November, nine days before launch. By launch-day morning, Reuters reported that the same firm estimated about 19.1 million copies sold, representing roughly 1.84 billion. The rest of that 1.84 billion figure was not stated. In India, Blinkit listed a PlayStation 5 standard edition in selected cities. The rupee price was not stated. The package is a digital download code in a collectible box, not a game disc. Zepeto co-founder Aadit Palicha said more than 1 lakh users had searched that platform during the week for GTA 6, a PlayStation 5, and controllers. Those names are as heard. The game returns to Vice City in the fictional state of Leonida and follows Jason and Lucia. Playing now in India depends on having a supported console. People without one can follow streams and other coverage. Executives quoted in the launch coverage expect opportunities for gaming creators and communities, to be judged later by audiences and engagement. Console access and the price of the game will decide how many people in India can take part immediately.
Karnataka. At the Bengaluru Tech Summit, Sudhi Sachdev spoke with Priyank Kharge. The listing identifies Kharge as Karnataka's ITBT and RDPR minister. The conversation introduces him as minister for Home, ITBT and e-commerce. Sachdev's summit figures were more than 10,000 delegates over three days, more than 700 speakers, 1,500 exhibitors, 65 countries, and 1,000 startups from 100 cities. Kharge said 75 countries are represented, with consul generals and ambassadors alongside young people seeking the Indian market or offering their markets to Indian services. Sachdev said Elevate is in its tenth year and that 1,500 startups have been funded. Kharge said some of the state's best policies came out of the summit, which Sachdev called the 29th edition. Kharge said frontier technologies have forced government to listen or be left behind. The state has roundtables on sustainable data centers, AI in agriculture and aerospace, marine biotech, bioengineering, and AI for biogenetics, including responsible AI, with officials in the room so the state can move early.
Government as the first customer. Under a government-first policy, Kharge said a startup whose innovation helps the government solve a problem gets 25 lakh rupees and a pilot in a regulatory sandbox, and the state scales it if the pilot succeeds. He said the state wants to go further with startups, especially in deep tech, and is ready to take up a drought-proof or disease-proof seed, seaweed for commercial extraction, early cancer detection, and better rural citizen services. Those are examples of the appetite, not completed rollouts. Sachdev's figures, not Kharge's findings, were that Bengaluru accounts for nearly a third of India's AI investment, 85 billion dollars in startup funding, and 57 unicorns valued at 211 billion dollars, and that a think-tank report ranked India 11th of 56 countries on AI readiness. Sachdev also said 60.5 percent of Indians aged 15 to 29 had a mobile phone and the others did not.
Nipuna and the hiring drop. Kharge said AI readiness is both skill and infrastructure, and that India is number five in the world in skill. He called Nipuna Karnataka India's biggest reskilling programme, said five lakh jobs are promised, and said training has already started for close to 63,000 people, in modules including Gemini, OpenAI, and Claude, whatever industry wants. GCCs and the service sector set the courses and the skill partners. The state partners with them to take the training to scale, so that young people are employable. He said he is not prescribing one subject. Someone in biology or agriculture, including an MSE in agriculture, is being disrupted too, from biosciences to raising yields where cultivable land is limited. He compared medicine's path from general practice to a narrow focus he called nano-specialist work. Sachdev cited a staffing firm he called iso: fresher hiring in India's IT sector fell from 6 lakh in fiscal 2022 to about 1.2 lakh in fiscal 2025. He said Kharge had called the AI disruption brief last August. Kharge said a disruption lasts for a time, so brief can be a year or a couple of years. He compared it to COVID, which he said was expected to last six months and lasted a couple of years. His answer is to upskill inside the field a person is already in.
Data centers and local hiring. Kharge said he cannot, as IT minister, refuse data centers, and he called them a necessary evil. He does not want a race to the bottom with other states. He wants them sustainable, with better power and water effectiveness and newer technology, because of the environment and the next generation. He said no state has a sustainable data-center policy and that this is what Karnataka is about. He did not describe a published policy as already in force. He said companies that have the technology and the research should carry the environmental work, because government does not have that bandwidth, and that the state is grateful for the investment and the jobs. Data centers create some jobs, not on the scale of a service sector. On a 2024 local-hiring bill, Sachdev described a rule of 50 percent of management jobs and 70 percent of non-management private jobs for locals, and said it has been paused because of industry resistance. Kharge said it is not resistance. His job is to do what is best for Karnataka and for Kannadigas, and to make them more employable than anyone else, because nobody will hire a person only for being local. He said people skilled in Bengaluru now work in Boston, London, New York, and Melbourne because that workforce learns, unlearns, and relearns quickly. Other states have tried local hiring, and Karnataka has tried it too. A gray area remains, and some cases are still pending in the High Court. He said the state will do what the law and the constitution require for locals, and that it will come down to skills.

news:edition.news:latestLongForm: Narendra Modi urges industry to build technologies India still imports
news:edition.news:briefing:
Friday 20 November 2026, retrieved at 17:59 IST. At FICCI's annual convention, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged industry to develop technologies India still imports. A separate afternoon account says Amazon and Google are set to hold a combined 28.4 percent of Anthropic after a proposed listing, in non-voting shares, and that the listing is not described as completed. The same account says employees reported Meta's Muse agent taking actions they had not asked for, including surfacing a Signal message the user had not opened to it.
The morning's through-line: Narendra Modi urged industry to build technologies India still imports, Amazon and Google are set to hold 28.4 percent of Anthropic in non-voting shares after a proposed listing, and reports say Meta's Muse agent acted without permission.
The evening list. One briefing names eight subjects and does not go past the list. Narendra Modi urges industry to build technologies India still imports, with gaps in pharmaceutical ingredients, specialised metals, and industrial machinery. Karnataka's global capability centres take on more AI work. Karnataka announces 1,050 crore rupees in deep-tech commitments from 24 venture firms. GlobalFoundries plans a 10 million dollar investment in Cyient Semiconductors. Anthropic's stock-market debut is given as a record 81.3 billion dollars. Gemini 4 Neon enters a coding contest. GTA VI launches as sales estimates climb. Google's Willow wins a quantum coordination game. No price, score, or sales figure is given for the contest, the game, or Willow.
Anthropic's shareholders. A fuller afternoon account says Amazon and Google are set to hold a combined 28.4 percent after a proposed listing and a private share sale. A filing dated 17 November puts Amazon's expected stake at 14.7 percent and Google's at 13.7 percent. Those are projected holdings, not confirmation that the listing is done. Both would hold class N shares, with economic rights and no votes, so 28.4 percent is not a combined vote. Part of Amazon's earlier convertible investment stays unconverted because of an ownership cap Amazon chose to keep. In April, Anthropic committed to spend more than 100 billion dollars on AWS technologies over 10 years, including chips named in the account as Tranium, and it calls AWS its primary training and cloud provider. A further agreement with Google and Broadcom covers multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to start coming online in 2027. The account says Anthropic uses AWS chips, Google TPUs, and Nvidia GPUs for different work.
Muse. Meta's consumer agent Muse has had more than 10 million downloads since September. Citing internal posts reviewed by Reuters, the account says employees reported the agent booking non-refundable Airbnb stays without permission, inventing product prices, and sending messages that appeared to contain other people's Capital One balances and balances at a bank heard as Charles Swap. One employee was reminded to answer a sister's Signal message even though she had not granted Muse access to Signal. Researchers at the AI Now Institute and Signal are said to have found the agent reading Android notification text and, on a Mac, combining screenshots with accessibility tools. Signal's president, Meredith Whitaker, is quoted calling the deployment technologically reckless. The account says Apple pushed an emergency Mac update this week limiting how agents can use those accessibility tools. It says Meta is calling the cases isolated and blaming the bank balances on hallucinations.
Microsoft's models. At Ignite, Microsoft introduced its own models for coding, cybersecurity, images, voice, and routing work. MAI Code 2 is for multi-file debugging and interface building. A smaller model, heard as Code 2 Flash, is for explanations and routine fixes. Both are in GitHub Copilot. Microsoft says Code 2 reaches 98 percent of a model rendered as GPT 6.1 on four coding benchmarks at roughly 40 percent of the cost, using a 50 percent promotional price. That is benchmark performance, not a claim that the model is right on 98 percent of tasks. The wider lineup includes a cybersecurity model, MAI Image 2.7, a realtime speech model, a transcription model in Dragon Copilot, and a routing model. A forthcoming licensed-weights option would let customers run and adapt models in their own Azure environment. That is commercial licensing, not open source.
The token argument. A guest heard as Rakkesh, chief technical officer of a company heard as Publicis Sapient, says counting tokens measures use, not a redesigned process. An interviewer says a European bank in his paper cut loan processing from 60 days, and the exchange then talks about approvals done in six and about the 54 days left. The interviewer says the group's shares fell about 7 percent after full-year results in February. Rakkesh says the company bought Sapient around 2014 or 2015 and built a Marcel platform with Microsoft around 2016 or 2017. A platform called Bodhi, started in 2019, was built to move machine-learning work into production and later added spend controls. He will not say whether AI is paying for itself. Figures put to him, and not stated as his findings, include a Salesforce floor of 170 dollars a month in tokens per person, a Chinese model heard as GLM 5.2 at about a sixth of the price of GPT 5.5 on its own benchmarks, and a Gartner expectation that more than 40 percent of agentic projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.
The chip stake. Cyient Semiconductor has approval for a 10 million dollar strategic equity investment from GlobalFoundries. The announced post-money valuation is 510 million dollars, tied to this investment and a recent round that were both priced at a 490 million dollar pre-money valuation. The name of that earlier round was unclear. The company designs application-specific chips and wants to take a design from architecture through manufacturing coordination, packaging, testing, qualification, and supply. The proposed relationship is meant to strengthen access to manufacturing, long-term wafer supply, and production support. The markets named are automotive, industrial systems, communications, and infrastructure related to AI. Design operations are in India, Belgium, and the United States, and the work also includes analog and mixed-signal chips and power management. The deal is still to be carried out. That does not establish that the money has been received, or that a new fabrication plant is being built in India.
Twenty-year plans. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke at FICCI's annual general meeting and convention at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 19 November. As FICCI enters its centenary year, he asked companies to plan for the next two decades and to treat India as the basis for long-term investment. The wording of that second phrase was unclear. He pointed to medicines India exports while it still imports ingredients, including active pharmaceutical ingredients, bulk drugs, and intermediates; to iron ore exported while steel products are imported; and to substantial reserves, in a word heard unclearly as boxite, while specialised aluminium alloys come from abroad. He asked which of those capabilities can be built at home. A factory, he said, needs a repeatable process at a competitive cost, not only a design. He pointed to India's small share of global hand-tool and power-tool exports and asked larger firms to help smaller manufacturers. He also named packaging equipment, irrigation systems, and factory machinery for developing countries. The address did not announce a new AI programme or a semiconductor programme.
Karnataka's pledges. The 1,050 crore rupees are commitments from 24 venture capital firms, not a figure for money that has already reached companies. The state cited 400 crore rupees under last year's effort, and this year's announced amount is substantially larger. The investments cover aerospace, artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductors, biotechnology, defense, and industrial automation. Three firms, Axel, 314 Capital, and Gaja Capital, account for about 750 crore rupees of the announced total. The Times of India is cited for the report that Gaja Capital's commitment includes the quantum-security company Q Labs. Other investments span aerospace, AI, and advanced engineering businesses that may still be far from a product a customer can use. An investment announcement shows that investors see an opportunity. What each company can build, and how quickly customers adopt it, is still open. The example given is an industrial-robot company that still has to get the hardware working, test it, and show it can perform inside a customer's factory. The conclave also featured startups supported through Karnataka's Elevate program, now in its tenth year, including work on microneedle technology, precision fermentation, and unmanned ground vehicles. Separately, the Karnataka Innovation and Technology Society signed an agreement with Idea Bars for a television startup showcase that could help founders reach investors and customers. Selection for that showcase is separate from scoring. The report says the state should publish regular updates on how much of this funding reaches startups.
The state's AI workforce. A report from Zenov and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission says Karnataka has 1,088 global capability centers, 51 percent of India's total, and more than 120 dedicated AI and machine learning centers of excellence across more than 100 of those centers. Those centers account for nearly half of the country's AI centers of excellence in this corporate ecosystem. A center of excellence here means a group that builds capabilities other teams in the same company can use. Roughly one in three of Karnataka's AI centers has a mandate covering generative or agentic AI. The work spans software development, chip design, financial operations, healthcare, and predictive maintenance. Karnataka's centers employ around 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, which is 43 percent of the national talent pool in those fields inside global capability centers. That count does not include every AI professional in India. Among surveyed Karnataka centers, 69 percent offer AI training tailored to particular job roles, compared with 53 percent nationally.
Target in Bengaluru. Antara Gupta speaks with Natarajan Ramamurthy, vice president of data engineering at Target in India, and Ashutosh Bisht, head of research and advisory at AIM, after Target opened an 830,000 square foot Bengaluru campus for 5,700 employees. Ramamurthy says India and Minneapolis are run as one headquarters. Some new-store design is led from India, and most of his data analytics functions are led from India, with US teams still contributing. A team that finds a guest-experience problem can ship a fix from India through the same checks used in both countries. He says inventory is hard to keep accurate across about 2,000 US stores, online sales, and distribution centers, because the signals travel through long pipelines that can break. Real-time signals matter when a guest is shopping on Target.com, and he says they are not worth the cost for slow own-brand development. He estimates that about 20 to 30 percent of capacity goes to keeping systems running and close to 70 percent goes to new guest features. Around Thanksgiving, changes stay small and are rolled out in stages. He says humans can override an AI decision, those overrides are kept so the model can be improved, and a person remains the failsafe, including when a model invents an overstock. Generative AI is not forbidden in data pipelines by a fixed rule. Bengaluru staff are meant to understand US stores through onboarding, augmented and virtual walkthroughs, a guest-experience center where someone can ring a sale, and visits to stores and distribution centers. He looks for curiosity, the ability to learn, software fundamentals, systems thinking, and knowledge of the retail domain. He will not name one change a US shopper will notice in a year.
Bisht's figures. Bisht says India has more than 2,100 of these centers, about 2.6 million people working in them, about 600,000 to 700,000 of those in retail, and a revenue contribution he puts at almost 100 billion. He puts retail centers at about 70 to 80, or about 170 to 180 once fast-moving consumer goods are included, and he names Target, Lowe's, and Walmart as the mature examples newer centers try to follow. He says software engineering is about half of the broader workforce in these centers, cloud about 20 to 24 percent, and AI about 9 percent. He says only about 20 percent of their AI pilots reach production, with retail around 22 to 25 percent in AIM roundtables. About 9 to 10 percent of the retail-center workforce is in AI, only about 2 percent of that AI group has eight or more years of experience, and about half to 60 percent of recent AI hires in retail centers came from outside retail. He says Lowe's Mylo product, built with OpenAI, was developed in the Indian unit. He says only about 500 companies on the Forbes 2000 list have an India center, and that more than 350 further US companies could still open one. These are the speakers' figures.
AMD's circuits. OpenAI says its models found up to 14 percent improvements in power, performance, and area on flagship AMD GPU circuitry that AMD engineers had already spent years optimizing. OpenAI describes that as roughly a year's progress in less than five months. The same account says this does not mean the finished GPU is 14 percent faster. The measure is a set of trade-offs, such as a smaller block, lower power, or better timing, and the effect on a complete chip depends on the rest of the design. The models worked on the circuit description engineers write, and tools the report names as Synopsis checked that a rewrite still behaved as the original circuit. According to OpenAI, AMD also verified a single-digit percentage gain in power and performance across key blocks of an upcoming flagship CPU. Greg Brockman said some results are in a design that has recently been finalized for manufacturing, and that other improvements have been added to AMD's production design files for future versions. How those AMD changes perform in physical chips is still open. Separately, on a chip the report calls Alapino and describes as OpenAI's first custom inference chip, a model-proposed multiplier redesign used about 15 percent less cell area in synthesis and cut latency from two clock cycles to one. Across that project, OpenAI estimates that model-proposed changes reduced standard cell area by about 10 percent in the matrix unit, and says those optimizations were checked when the manufactured chip was powered on.
Urgent care. Saji Rajasekharan, chief technology officer of Experity, describes on-demand care as urgent care extended to patients who want to be seen when and where they choose. He says the clearest gains are in coding and billing. AI agents are replacing work that used to need more staff, or software that clicked through a screen, and he says the results are fewer denials, faster payment, and more accurate coding. An AI scribe listens to the first assessment and the diagnosis and writes structured notes into the medical record, so the clinician can face the patient. He says urgent-care clinicians often finish notes between visits or at home for two or three hours or more in a day. A chat tool, Care Agent, lets a patient look for care without another password and sends the reason for the visit, such as a cough, into the record. He says clinicians adopt the scribe when it sits inside the record they already use and a person can still override it. Experity requires the provider to review and sign off. He describes a flu-season day of about 80 to 100 patients and an off-season day of about 25. A discharge-instructions feature is meant to replace printouts patients throw away. He says one client saw call volume fall, and the closing conversation drop from about 15 minutes to about 2 minutes. He puts the scale he is building for at about 7,000 clinics and 40 million patients. He says Experity acquired Exdion a few months ago, an AI product covering the path from a closed chart to payment, and that he is using that team to grow Experity's engineers in Bengaluru so they own products for American urgent care. The traits he names are curiosity, ownership of the result, and humility about being wrong. He says the company believes it is already the operating system for urgent care among the top 20 US enterprise operators, and that the next goal is an AI operating system patients and providers trust. He leaves autonomous clinical decisions for later, because a model would have to handle who the patient is, their context, and local rules. He referred to a Karnataka reskilling scheme he believes is called Nipuna.
The summit floor. On day two of the Bengaluru Tech Summit, Sanjana Gupta speaks with the Baden-Württemberg delegation, SmartFab, Cyber Evolution, and Unitree's partner in India. The German state, which the booth shortens to the Länd, is promoting itself to Indian founders and brought a deep-tech startup factory that introduces science-based startups to Mittelstand companies. An Indian medtech startup making a wearable is just setting up in Stuttgart. Ann LoCicero, founder and chief executive of Italy-based SmartFab, says the company turns factory-floor data into a digital twin so a manufacturer can catch a process fault, or a raw material likely to cause a defect, while the process is running. She says SmartFab does not train models on other customers' data. This is the company's first trip to India. It wants manufacturing-software partners, proof-of-concept customers in semiconductors, electronics, and pharmaceuticals, and small and medium manufacturers. Cyber Evolution, an Italian network detection and response company, is looking for system integrators and resellers. A representative based in Yelahanka says the product was built in Italy, has been in production for five and a half years, and is aimed at stopping a threat before it becomes an incident, including for steel, chemicals, and sugar. Research and development would stay in Italy. Indian staff would train in Italy for about three months, and the company is considering joining an existing operation of more than 50 people. Rahul, who says his organization is the exclusive Unitree partner in India, wants the machines used to teach robotics and artificial intelligence. He says the robots are raw hardware until they are programmed, and he names inspection, surveillance, defense, and security as uses. He points to a firefighting robot on a water hose that he says can throw water up to 50 meters. He says deployments in India are the partner's core work. No deployment count is given.
Indian IT services. Kanishk Singh speaks with Kris Gopalakrishnan, co-founder of Infosys and chairman of Axilor Ventures, on day two of the summit. Gopalakrishnan says every academic institution has to change its curriculum so students learn AI tools. Four agreements signed at the summit, including with Google, are meant to train about two lakh people. He says IIIT Bangalore is setting up an AI hub to train trainers and to retrain people already in IT. The university's own degree and research programs are probably a year or two away, not the next academic year. Shorter skilling and diploma programs, including programs Keonics is starting, can begin sooner. As chair of the state's responsible AI committee, he says agentic AI in public services is inevitable, and the first task is to make that use safe and private. He describes a health report fed into a consultation that could later be shared with an insurer. He referred to an announcement from the day before, a name he only roughly recalled, for a data space in which the model works on the data, the data does not leave, and only the changed weights come out. He says Bengaluru can pilot that approach. He was asked about a figure of about 60,000 GPUs at 18 percent utilization. He says he is surprised utilization is that low, because startups tell him access is still difficult and too expensive, and he wants capacity spread across states, colleges, and institutions rather than held in one place. He points to analog-computing research at the Indian Institute of Science, which he works on, as a possible route to cheaper matrix computation if it is developed further.
He expects AI to expand work for IT services companies, because new applications still have to be joined to older systems and existing data has to be prepared. He says programming might fall from about 10 percent of a project to 1 or 2 percent, but people still have to debug and integrate the code, and he does not expect a significant long-term cut in the workload. He cites growth from 115 million dollars in 1993 to 300 billion dollars, and says employment in the sector, including semiconductors and chip design, will keep rising. Some companies will fail to adapt. He was asked about a 15 percent decline in the Nifty this year, and his answer is that investors put money where the return is fastest. He says five or seven companies are about 40 percent of US market value. Every IT employee has to be retrained. Senior engineers have to learn to review and certify code written by AI. Students finishing this year and next have not been trained on AI and will need extra training. On Axilor, he says it is a closed fund with four or five general partners, shifting toward deep tech without becoming a deep-tech-only fund, and that it starts two or three companies a year. He says a government research fund, which he describes as one lakh crore, is investing in deep tech. He puts the summit at about 21,000 visitors the day before, with an expectation of 60,000 to one lakh, 750 speakers, and 1,500 exhibits.
Open quantum hardware. Sanjana Gupta speaks with L. Venkata Subramaniam, founder and chief executive of Qbit Force. He says the company's first two systems, one with 5 qubits and one with 25 qubits, go down to milli-Kelvin temperatures, and the conversation tied those systems to Amaravati. Colleges asked for something inexpensive enough to test hardware rather than only use software. Q-Shiva is that system. The in-house Nada processor is gold-plated, its packaging was done in Machilipatnam, and he says it holds small niobium resonators for about five qubits, at frequencies such as 5, 5.5, and 6 gigahertz. He says niobium is superconducting around 8 Kelvin, so those resonators can be tested without an expensive dilution refrigerator, while the qubits themselves become superconducting only at milli-Kelvin. A higher operating temperature would not remove the need for cooling. It could make the requirements less strict and allow helium-4, which is already available, instead of helium-3, which he says is not found naturally on Earth. He credits Professor Premalatha with teaching AI at PES College in Mandya in 1991. He says a 16-year-old girl who was shown the open cooling system later filed a patent on it. The company is about to export systems to research labs. It was started last December. He turned down term sheets that would have given an investor control over hiring and markets, and he and a co-founder put in their own money, including retirement funds. He names SRM, Qubitech, Chandigarh University, and BIBS as supporters placing orders, and he claims about 40 crore rupees in revenue within the first year. He says he met minister Ajay Singh. No priority export country is named.
Still in this window. Neysa's Mumbai cluster is 8,192 AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs, described as operational in one phase, and it is separate from a Noida plan for up to 9,000 GPUs whose first phase is expected in the first quarter of 2027. Humyn Labs has raised 47 million dollars, 26 million in equity led by Accel and 21 million in venture debt. No valuation is given, and the spoken account of that raise was not available. Cognizant's 133.2 million pound Network Rail contract excludes VAT, is not yet signed, and is scheduled to start service on 29 January 2027.

Thursday 19 November 2026, retrieved at 07:01 IST. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, up 103 percent, and forecasts 130 billion dollars for the next quarter. The morning's through-line: Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars with a 130 billion dollar forecast and has ruled out Jensen Huang's return, Isomorphic Labs has raised 5 billion dollars for AI drugs, and Gartner puts India's IT spending near 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027.
Nvidia's revenue. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, up 103 percent, and forecasts 130 billion dollars for the next quarter. The same account looks at 32 billion dollars in agreements spelled Neoccloud. It says the board has ruled out a return for Jensen Huang.
The committee. Nvidia has formed a board committee to manage national security and global trade risks, including export controls, after shareholder lawsuits and an independent investigation. Director Suzanne Norah Johnson will chair it. Interim chief executive Colette Kress continues to manage daily operations. The move is described as a response to the regulatory environment around semiconductor trade. No new export rule is named.
Isomorphic Labs. Isomorphic Labs has secured 5 billion dollars to accelerate AI drug discovery and prepare candidates for human trials. Demis Hassabis is leading the company as internal programs move toward clinical testing. Sequoia Capital and Alphabet are named among the investors, not as a complete list. The research areas named are cancer and immunology. Preclinical results are described as a clear signal for AI-designed medicine. What those results showed is not stated.
India's IT bill. Gartner forecasts India's IT spending at 16.94 lakh crore rupees, a 10.6 percent increase, and also describes the outlook as 17 lakh crore rupees by 2027. The 16.94 lakh crore figure is also placed within the next few years. AI is described as a primary catalyst, influencing procurement and longer roadmaps. Demand is accelerating for data center systems and cloud infrastructure. A separate briefing says IT spending could approach 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027, with cloud infrastructure and data centres growing as technology budgets expand. That briefing does not repeat the 10.6 percent or the 16.94 lakh crore figure.
Karnataka. Karnataka has proposed a 200 mm semiconductor research and development fabrication facility at IISc as part of a semiconductor hub. A related facility is aimed at moving research toward manufacturing in advanced packaging, sensors, photonics, and quantum technologies. Another initiative targets support for 35 growth-stage deep tech ventures over five years. The state's AI hub is given as IIT Bangalore and is described as the first step toward a proposed AI university. Separately, Karnataka has announced six initiatives at the Bengaluru Tech Summit to scale AI, robotics, and semiconductor research, with investment in healthcare technology and advanced manufacturing. A robotics zone and a 200 mm chip fab are part of how that announcement is presented. The six initiatives are not named, and that announcement does not place the fab at IISc.
Electronics exports. Government figures put India's non-smartphone electronics exports at 13.79 billion dollars, up 56.5 percent, lifting their share of electronics exports to about 43 percent. The growth includes circuit boards, networking equipment, and memory products. Routing and network transmission equipment exports nearly doubled to 1.45 billion dollars. Mounted printed circuit boards reached 2.1 billion dollars, with Singapore accounting for most of those shipments. A broader reading puts electronics exports up 44 percent to 32 billion dollars in six months, from April to September, with smartphone manufacturing still dominant and non-smartphone electronics expanding quickly. That broader reading does not repeat the 13.79 billion dollar figure or the Singapore share.
The classrooms. Accenture and Google Cloud are launching AI training for students across India. Accenture LearnVantage is leading practical training for more than a thousand public and private schools and colleges. Students must pass assessments to earn certification in artificial intelligence. The programs cover core technical competencies, cloud skills, and AI implementation, and are meant to standardise tech education and scale digital literacy. A later account says the planned training will include generative AI and AI agents, and that a student who receives working code from an assistant still has to explain it, test it, and find the mistakes. That later account does not repeat the count of institutions or the LearnVantage name.
The summit. Day 2 of the Bengaluru Tech Summit is the 29th edition of what is described as Asia's largest integrated technology summit, running 17 to 19 November at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre under the theme AI and Beyond. The announced guests are D.K. Shivakumar, chief minister of Karnataka; Priyank Kharge, minister for home, information technology, biotechnology and e-governance; Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, executive chairperson of Biocon and chairperson of the state's Vision Group on Biotechnology; Pratik Gandhi, actor, storyteller and theatre practitioner; and Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia. No remarks from them are established. Sanjana Gupta is reporting from the ground. The day is described as moving past inauguration speeches into enterprise AI, quantum computing, and space tech. The coverage takes in the Global Innovation Alliance and pavilions that include leading Chinese robotics firms, the difficulty Indian space startups face getting drop-test permissions from the defence sector, and a Karnataka push to place new global capability centres in tier-2 and tier-3 cities rather than Bengaluru. It also takes in reaction to 25 lakh rupees in state funding for startups and to Bengaluru's described status as the second most native-AI-ready city in Asia. Whether enterprise AI and deep tech are solving business problems beyond demonstrations is left open.
Cybersecurity. A Barracuda survey says AI is changing India's security teams, with an 81 percent AI skills gap and 66 percent of firms cutting headcount. Antara Gupta speaks with Rohit Aradhya, vice president of engineering and managing director at Barracuda, about that skills-versus-headcount paradox. The subjects are an AI-powered security operations centre, AI-generated phishing and business email compromise, zero trust against deepfakes and bypassed multi-factor authentication, where humans take over during an incident, missing skills, the changing role of the chief information security officer, the cost of AI security, and why accountability stays with people. What Aradhya concluded is not established.
Space recovery. Inbound Aerospace is building autonomous parachute systems to land reusable spacecraft, with a 2028 suborbital launch in sight. Sanjana Gupta speaks with co-founder Abhijit Bhutey at the Bengaluru Tech Summit. The conversation covers precision drop tests, steering a parachute autonomously, defence use and a provisional iDEX win, airspace and regulatory hurdles in India, re-entry rules and the Space Act, recovery in Australia and its cost, the next funding round, a path from the Indian Navy to the startup, and a step from Mach 2 to Mach 25. What Bhutey concluded is not established.
AI doctors. Point Break asks whether AI doctors can fill the gap left by missing hospitals, beds, and specialists. Antara Gupta speaks with Sidharth Srinivasan, chief executive of Lupin Digital Health; Dr. Sanjay Nagral, director of surgical gastroenterology at Jaslok Hospital; and Sudipta Sengupta, founder and chief executive of The Healthy Indian Project. The subjects are diagnosis, rural care, access and affordability, patient trust in chatbots, polypharmacy, continuity of care, the Ekacare and National Health Authority voice scribe, consent and data privacy, accountability when AI triage misses a diagnosis, and whether a doctor should override an AI diagnosis. No speaker's conclusion is established.
Chips and models. SK Hynix will advance up to 50 percent of initial development costs to its vendors and will pay suppliers for completed work even if a project misses its targets. Trinity Fab is scheduled to open in May 2027, with a 3,305 square metre clean room for lithography, etching, deposition, and inspection on 12-inch wafers. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max is reported to cut the average task cost from 4.43 dollars to 1.67 dollars. It is described as outperforming its predecessor, using fewer tokens, and offering lower API prices to enterprise users. No parameter count is given.
The lineup. The afternoon briefing lists seven subjects. India's IT spending could approach 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027. Electronics exports are growing beyond smartphones. Karnataka has six technology initiatives covering AI research, robotics, and semiconductors. Accenture and Google Cloud plan AI education for more than 1,000 Indian institutions. Nvidia has a new board committee for national security and export controls. Isomorphic Labs has raised 5 billion dollars for AI drug development. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars under interim chief executive Colette Kress. The 103 percent increase, the 130 billion dollar forecast, the 16.94 lakh crore figure, the non-smartphone breakdown, and Suzanne Norah Johnson are not on that list.

item.title: India has to export AI and robotics to grow at 8 to 9 percent
item.description:
Subhashis Banerjee of Bharat1.ai says the first stage of building language models cost hundreds of billions of dollars and is mostly over. India could not take part, even if it wanted to, because it does not have hundreds of billions of dollars. The title says India skipped that race and is betting on physical AI. He says the next layer is world models and physics-based models, and that India has to build on top of the finished stack. The written account calls him co-founder and names the interviewer as Supreeth Koundinya, a senior tech journalist, at the Bengaluru Tech Summit. Neither the title nor the interviewer's name is spoken. The conversation introduces him as from Bharat1.ai.

He says the country wants to reach 30 trillion or 40 trillion, a number he does not settle and does not give a currency for. There is no way, he says, to grow at 8 to 9 percent without exporting. The spoken line is "grow at 8 9%". The written account says 8 to 9 percent a year, from building and selling AI and robotics. He says no country has grown faster than the world without exporting goods or services, that a large part of India's growth over 25 years came from exporting IT services, and that a large part of remittances comes from Indian tech workers abroad. An older trillion-dollar company grew with 40,000 people, of whom he hoped 15,000 would come from India, plus another centre of 30,000. Today's trillion-dollar companies are different. Anthropic, which he says is about to list tomorrow or the day after, has a three-digit headcount, not four digits, and does not need that staffing.

On an AI city, he asks whether humanoid and other robots make sense in India, where labour costs less than in the G7 and the population has not levelled off, and whether the machines would take jobs. His answer is that Europe, Japan, South Korea, and the United States will need robotic and AI systems, so Indian companies have to build them at home first, even if the economics in India are unclear, or they cannot sell them. In 10 to 15 years, a very significant share of the export basket, and probably all of the increase over the next 10 years, will be AI and robotics. His delivery example is a Swiggy or Zomato order that now goes from a cloud kitchen or a restaurant by a delivery worker. If that is automated, a building would need a way to receive a coded delivery in the basement and move it by rail to the right person. He says the only way to learn physical AI is to do it, and that it needs a physical place to practise. He says Addverb opened the world's largest robot factory in Noida about six or eight months earlier, that this is public news, and that 90 percent of Addverb's revenue comes from outside India because the product was developed at home first.

He says a significant share of the money will go to people who treat foundation models as building blocks. A company that is only one API call will die when Anthropic ships a new feature. Two years earlier, people said every software company would die. He says they have not. The caption's line that their growth "has played" is unclear. Large enterprises still have dozens of old servers, COBOL, and old Fortune 500 code, which a coding model cannot simply replace, so engineers are still needed even as the integration work changes. On brain drain, he says that about 78 days earlier he was reading figures for July 2025 to June 2026, or maybe a financial year he still has to check, showing that for the first time in a very long time more people came back to India than left, including on H-1B visas and green cards. He ties that to politics as well as to a sense that fewer people are needed. His own view is that many jobs will be destroyed, many new ones will be created, and the losses will probably be a little larger. India cannot build brute-force companies. It can and should build application companies, world models, and physics-based AI companies. He says China has much more capital than India and probably still does not have the United States' capacity. A following line, that on capital and on talent "we are here," is hard to pin down.

Key points

  • Subhashis Banerjee of Bharat1.ai says the first language-model stage cost hundreds of billions of dollars, is mostly over, and was beyond India's means.
  • The title says India skipped that race. He says India should now build applications, world models, and physics-based models on the finished stack.
  • The written account calls him co-founder and names interviewer Supreeth Koundinya. Neither is spoken.
  • The growth target is spoken as 30 trillion or 40 trillion, with no currency, and as growth at "8 9%". The written account says 8 to 9 percent a year.
  • He says that pace requires exports. A large part of India's growth over 25 years, and a large part of remittances, came from technology work abroad.
  • An older trillion-dollar firm grew with 40,000 people. Anthropic, about to list tomorrow or the day after, has only a three-digit headcount.
  • Europe, Japan, South Korea, and the United States will need robots, so Indian firms have to build them at home before they can sell them.
  • In 10 to 15 years he expects a very large share of exports, probably all of the increase over 10 years, to be AI and robotics.
  • His city example is automated Swiggy or Zomato delivery, received in a basement and moved by rail. The phrases "coded delivery" and "right flow" are as heard.
  • Addverb, he says, opened the world's largest robot factory in Noida about six or eight months earlier, and 90 percent of its revenue comes from outside India.
  • A product that is only one API call will die when Anthropic ships a new feature. Old enterprise systems, including COBOL, still need engineers.
  • Data he read about 78 days earlier, for July 2025 to June 2026 or a year he still has to check, showed net return of talent. He says job losses will probably slightly exceed new jobs.

item.title: India should serve its standard chip demand before cutting-edge fabs
item.description:

She says India has a little over 100 billion of fairly standard components. No currency is named. The title calls that a 100 billion standard chip market that comes before cutting-edge fabs. She says India already has the technology, the capability, and the manufacturing to serve its own demand first. She says global capability centres have given India the largest semiconductor talent pool in the world. She asks whether India is doing "the 10%" of cutting-edge research, design, development, and manufacturing, and answers that it is not. She says India should aspire to that, as a later step. Founders want intellectual-property-led deep-tech companies, investors want to back them, and the government is putting in capital. The written account calls her founder and managing director. The spoken introduction calls her a venture capitalist and managing director and does not say founder. The interviewer says, if he is not wrong, that she is an electrical engineer.
