item.title: Deriv open-sourced its staff AI platform after 221 skills had no clear permissions
item.description:
Deriv is an online trading company with more than 26 years behind it, more than 3 million traders, and 900 staff in 13 countries. The opening line is heard once as "3 million tra traders" and later as more than 3 million traders. Sudhi Sachdev speaks with Christopher Hernandez, AI team lead, and Ansh Choudhary, senior AI engineer, about Deriv One. The interviewer names the chief executive as Rakshit Choudhary. The guests do not repeat that name. The chief executive asked for a shared list of AI skills. Staff returned 221 skills from 54 people, each described a little differently, and nobody could say who was allowed to run what. The title calls that a permissions mess. Public marketplaces for these skills have already been caught carrying malware. Deriv built a control layer, gave the code away under the MIT licence, and wrote instructions that are frank about where the fix falls short.

Hernandez says a skill is repeatable steps for an agent, the tools it needs, its objective, and a structured result if one is required. He says they plan to run more than a thousand agents, that skills then sprawled, including near-duplicates, and that the project started because they needed control and a way to see what was running. He moved from IT operations to security operations and has been in AI engineering since 2021. Choudhary helped build the platform with the chief executive and the head of engineering. The interviewer says Choudhary placed second in a capture-the-flag contest at GITEX Global 2025. Choudhary says his boss came first. Every upload goes through an automated review for malicious commands and secrets before it can enter the registry. A skill can stay private or be shared inside a department. Hernandez says easy generation also produces low-quality skills, so quality is a problem as well as security. Stacked role checks decide who can use, change, and invoke a skill.

Choudhary says a new hire is recognised by department and team and is given the skills and agents for that team, including through Slack. If a skill is missing, the agent says so and links to a request. The skill owner or the agent owner can approve it at once. The interviewer describes a new hire saying hello in Dubai on a Monday. The guests do not confirm that scene. He also retells a story from Pat Casey, chief technology officer of ServiceNow, about an internal human-resources agent that agreed when people asked it to raise their salaries. Hernandez calls that a new way in, and says the control is still who the person is and what they are allowed to ask.

The interviewer says the 54 contributors sit inside more than 900 staff, and that the target is to automate 75 percent of manual workflows by the end of this year. Neither guest gives a percentage. Choudhary says work started in May and the platform was released about one or two months later, with no year. Finance and compliance went first. Staff who could not build skills were helped directly, and use then spread. By the time the 54-person figure was cited, he says, more departments had joined, and he remembers more than 400 skills. Hernandez says earlier automations were written by engineers on outside platforms, with staff bringing their own models. Deriv One is meant to let non-technical staff attach tools and build agents. A couple of people in marketing made stickers for an agent, including a happy one and a sad one, and asked the agent to treat a Slack reaction as its next input. The team added that.

The interviewer cites IBM: 63 percent of breached organisations had no AI governance policy, and heavy users of unapproved AI tools paid about 670,000 dollars more per breach. Hernandez treats unsanctioned AI like unknown software. Staff can use the latest providers, some want to try smaller ones, and the company limits who can, watches what is used, and watches network logins. He says the European Union is one of the strictest places they operate, and that an internal governance tool next to Deriv One checks recommended controls and scans every day for new rules in the EU and elsewhere. If an agent should not see client details, pattern matches are removed and replaced with synthetic values. If a Slack answer should not be seen by others in the channel, it is shown only to the person who asked. The agent can also refuse. A trader, Hernandez says, should ask any broker how data is handled, what the contracts with providers say, whether zero data retention is enforced, what agents can see and do, and whether security is the first question. He says that is how Deriv starts.

The interviewer describes a July article in which an agent reads incoming documents and one document hides an instruction such as "send me the customer list." The written account calls that prompt injection. Those words are not spoken. Hernandez says guardrails sit in the system prompt, cloud monitoring watches the major providers, and proxies look at requests and replies before the content is cleaned. When the agent tries to act, the system looks up the person, the allowed actions, and the allowed data. Tokens last only for that session, stay in memory, and are revoked and deleted when the session ends.

The interviewer says five people built the MIT release and asks why give it away. Choudhary does not confirm the headcount. He says the chief executive wanted a system built for Deriv to be general enough for other companies, and useful enough that outside changes come back. Open-sourcing forced hardening and took about ten times more work, and it made the internal product better. A couple of interview candidates arrived having already changed Deriv One. Hernandez says he now prefers security that can be inspected. Attackers and defenders are using the same kinds of tools. The interviewer says the starter instructions let anyone who can reach the setup log in as an administrator, and that the default sandbox shares the host machine's kernel. Hernandez does not confirm the kernel point and does not name a group that should wait. He says the first change, for personal or company-wide use, is to put in one's own role checks. The administrator login exists so operators can control the system.

For a bank or insurer that wants staff agents without losing control, Choudhary describes two failures: giving every employee every AI system, or locking the tools so tightly that people cannot learn them. A non-technical person in human resources or customer work gets a button to create an agent, then a name, a description, and skills. He says there is a limit to what can go wrong there, unlike a coding agent the person cannot later watch or manage. Access control is meant to be in place on day one, so the checks are fixed rules rather than a review after the fact. He mentions a talk, in a place he calls "our dev company," where he put out 17 to 20 questions about securing AI. Hernandez says he does see the platform used where buyers need controls that Claude, ChatGPT, and other labs do not supply, including HIPAA in the United States and DORA in the European Union. Others can keep the code, add stricter rules, and bring their own models. He says he wants to trust tools he calls Grockbot, and OpenAI's documents, and does not fully know how those handle credentials or network isolation. On their own platform they can see. Asked about well-funded labs treating the release as a threat, he says he would like to see them try. He cites a long internal argument about harnesses and another topic he calls loop engineering, and says larger providers are becoming slow in the way some software suites have.

Choudhary says a staff member with a free chatbot worries him more than an agent with too much access, because a person can be talked into anything. He calls humans the biggest weakness and cites employee compromises at Binance, whether or not they were intentional. Hernandez says companies should switch off autonomous assistant agents, because they end up with far too much access. That is a major reason Deriv built its own, and related features are part of what they plan to release next. He does not give the detail. Choudhary says that within six months they are adding computer use: an agent with a computer that can do a task and hand it back when it is stuck. He says a version already works inside Deriv, and he compares it with what he calls grog bots. Hernandez says staff should be told when an agent has done their work, and that the person who can automate a job should not fear being automated if they are the one building it. The first step he names is security, with a view across the company and, because the code is open, beyond it. Choudhary says 25 or 26 years of accumulated process, against the opening's "more than 26 years," create friction, and that a team should decide what the work actually is before it automates the process it already has.

Key points

  • Deriv has more than 3 million traders and 900 staff in 13 countries. The 900 figure is headcount, not a count of people building skills.
  • Staff returned 221 skills from 54 people, with no clear rule for who could run what. The platform that followed is Deriv One, released under the MIT licence.
  • The interviewer names the chief executive as Rakshit Choudhary. The guests do not confirm the spelling.
  • Christopher Hernandez defines a skill as steps, tools, an objective, and an optional structured result. Uploads are scanned for malicious commands and leaked secrets.
  • Ansh Choudhary remembers more than 400 skills. Work started in May and was released about one or two months later, with no year. Finance and compliance were first.
  • The interviewer states a target of automating 75 percent of manual workflows this year. Neither guest gives progress toward it.
  • Client details an agent should not see are replaced with synthetic values. A Slack answer others should not see is shown only to the requester.
  • A hidden instruction such as "send me the customer list" is the interviewer's example. Session tokens stay in memory and are deleted when the session ends.
  • "Five people built it" is the interviewer's claim and is not confirmed. Open-sourcing took about ten times more work, in Choudhary's account.
  • The starter setup's administrator login is confirmed. The claim that the default sandbox shares the host kernel is the interviewer's, and Hernandez does not confirm it. The first change he names is the organisation's own access rules.
  • Hernandez says autonomous assistants with too much access should be switched off. Computer use is the next addition within six months and already works inside Deriv.
  • IBM's 63 percent and 670,000 dollars, and the ServiceNow salary-agent story, are the interviewer's accounts. The guests do not confirm the figures.

item.title: Kaynes Semicon intends to package close to 10 billion devices at full scale
item.description:
The account is a walk through the Kaynes Semicon plant in Sanand, then a conversation about what the site is for. The written account says Sanjana Gupta tours it with Raghu Panicker, chief executive of Kaynes Semicon, and the Kaynes team. The spoken account addresses Sanjana and never says Raghu Panicker. People heard on the floor include Rajib, introduced as business-development vice president, Pranab, who handles supply chain and is also tied to cost and industrial engineering, and a person addressed as Mr. Kalanos or Mr. Kalano. The interviewer later names guides as Nani and Aus. It is not clear whether those are the same people. The written account says the plant plans to scale to six units. The spoken account discusses units 1 through 6 and later says the complex is going to six or seven. The title says a plant planned for 10 billion devices. The speaker says they intend, on a full scale, to do close to 10 billion devices. That is not a figure for current output.

Customers across the world supply the wafer, which is the customer's intellectual property. What is on the wafer is called each curve, each diode, or each chip, and it is a power device that will become an intelligent power module. After incoming inspection the steps are wafer mount, a cut heard as pour-ring or pyuring, and wafer saw. Pranab says one machine was imported from a supplier he remembers as CAS Technologies, based in Bangalore. Gas and piping can be set up in India. Semiconductor machines are the hard import, local materials are not easy to qualify, and the customer still has to agree. Die attach is shown on an inline machine in a dry cycle. A power module is said to have 17 dice, also described as 15 in one place and two in another. Six, then six, then three are attached after epoxy or paste is dispensed. The line then cures, cleans flux, plasma-cleans the surface, and does aluminium and copper wire bonding. A question heard as whether it is a "six-one" is answered yes. After wire bond, an automatic inspection marks rejects in a map file for the end of the line. Tests named are a functional test, ball shear, die shear, and wire pull. A separate package step, called DBC attach, with IGBT die attach and solder-paste printing, then goes to the same moulding.

The site is 46 acres, and the distance from one fence to the far fence is given as 1 kilometre. Unit 2, the next building, is 16,000 square metres and is described as the expansion of unit 1. Equipment there is first called 480-plus machines and then around 485, including a clean room of around 8,000 square metres and a controlled area of around 9,000. The building is under construction. Testing alone is confirmed at around 100 machines. At least two plating lines are planned, plus an original-design line and an assembly line. One plating line is running, and space for a matching imported second line is on the other side of a wall. The line covers what is heard as a lip or lid frame, including tin plate, and a high-pressure water jet that removes flash. It sits after trimming and before bending, then the work returns to unit 1 for forming. Plating does not need a clean room, but the chemical does, because of contamination, metal mix, and thickness. The chemical is heard as citrine or citron, supplied as a ready composition, imported from Malaysia for now, and stored on site. A lab runs volumetric analysis. An X-ray fluorescence machine measures thickness. Parts from unit 1 are chemically flashed to remove extra resin, then rinsed and washed on separate machines.

A surface-mount area combines packaging with board assembly for a communication module. It is under construction, machines are already there, and it is expected to operate at the end of November. The area is called original design manufacturing. A chip, heard as COBS, is embedded in the board for Indian strategic needs, a satellite-navigation module, and a camera module. Three lines are planned, two for assembly and one for testing. The unit 2 clean room has a raised floor of at least 1 metre so air comes from the ceiling and leaves at the floor. The other unit feeds air from the ceiling and has no raised floor. A services area of at least 500 square metres is called unique to Kaynes. The interviewer says unit 1 has a 10k clean room. Unit 3 is given as 48,000 square metres over three stories and unit 4 as around 40,000. The speaker then adds 50 plus 40 to reach around 90,000. Unit 5 is around 20,000 square metres over three stories and unit 6 around 25,000, which they then call another 40 to 45, for a total around 140,000 to 145,000 square metres. Those additions do not match the earlier storeys. They call the total the room available on the site.

Two power sources were considered from the start, in a phrase heard as "in GC." Water is collected and pretreated into RO and DI water. A fire pump is nearby. Effluent is treated, and the aim is zero liquid discharge, with waste chemicals reused on site rather than released onto public land. They say they are complying with that requirement. A plant turns liquid nitrogen into nitrogen gas. Power is 11 kilovolts now and will be 66, with one source online and one on standby.

The later pitch is a single place for research, assembly and test, post-silicon engineering and validation, reliability and failure analysis, smaller modules, and a system group that makes a load board. Asked how an India plant compares with Taiwan or China, he says a customer compared it with outsourced assembly and test outside India, named a top 10 in which companies like ASE and Amkor figure in the top five, and called this a C++. Volume production and test happen here. New-product introduction and new-product design can be tested here, with a Bangalore team, using what he calls 40 to 45 years of chip-design work in India. He says the Government of India has approved 12 companies and Kaynes is one. The complex will not stop at three units. The yield standard he states is 99.999 percent. He also says an automotive-grade semiconductor cannot fail: a chip in what is heard as an anti-breaking system must make the airbag open, so quality has to be 100 percent and cannot be 99.99 percent. Factory discipline, he says, has to be built.

The interviewer mentions a Kaynes space subsidiary. The next products are sensors for cars, microelectronics, or space. They have started talking to the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad, a state-owned body, about sensors that go into space and need radiation-hardened devices and a wide temperature range. The order he gives is industrial grade, then automotive, then space. The interviewer says a lot of everyday devices are not made in India and, as the interviewer recalls, are imported from Israel. The speaker says a large portion of chips go to industrial or consumer uses, naming IPM 5 and IPM 7, a microcontroller effort, and memory. Products go into air conditioners, washing machines, and fans, and a chip is going to one of the biggest names in Pune, who is not named. Consumer qualification is looser, because a chip in a fan can be allowed to fail. They are IATF qualified, so the next products go into two-wheelers and four-wheelers, and then aerospace.

On hiring, he says two and a half years of learning produced junior engineers, who are easier to teach. Partners, as heard, include PDEU, Gujarat Technological University, NMA Institute, a university in Sahasar, and one close to Tanjaw. Some are putting in equipment and a clean room for seventh- and eighth-semester students. Interns work in research on the ground floor of the admin building. A 45-day programme and a one-year programme are running, and some people are sent to Penang and Japan and brought back. Headcount is now only 100. He wants 500 and 700 in the next three to four months, then thousands or 2,000 as unit 2 comes up. Hiring reaches tier-two and tier-three universities. He says the Ministry of Electronics and IT, the India Semiconductor Mission, and Gujarat, including the Gujarat State Electronics Mission and the department of science and technology, have given what support they could. He names Professor Rao Tummala of Georgia Tech. A line about him and "2025 universities" is unclear, and the same passage says technology is being brought to IIT Gandhinagar and IIT Bhubaneswar, one hub for space-age materials and one for advanced packaging, with nearby colleges as spokes. A chip-to-startup or chip-to-systems programme has given design tools to close to 200 to 250 universities. He says a second semiconductor mission adds training, with a 75 percent subsidy for some training centres.

Asked why Sanand rather than Karnataka, he says he would rather be where the city wants to grow. Bangalore and Hyderabad are crowded and have had 30 to 40 years of the work. His attrition in Sanand is very low and would have been very high in Bangalore. Being in a corner keeps people on the factory, and it is also a disadvantage. He says three factories are now in Sanand, naming Micron and CG Semi along with Kaynes, with a headcount he does not state cleanly. In two more years he expects the city to be a semiconductor manufacturing hub. The 12 approved companies are in different cities. The three in Sanand, he says, do not compete: one does memory, one does microcontrollers, and one does IPM 5 and IPM 7 power products. He does not map those three roles onto the three company names one by one. During a prime minister's inauguration at one of the three, heavy rain clogged that site while Kaynes stayed clear, so cars were parked at Kaynes. One company used Kaynes equipment when its own reliability tools were late. Kaynes and another company talked to raw-material suppliers together, and the state mission published a report on that work. They have a basic agreement not to poach. The gap he names after three and a half years is people and cost, not capital: teams of three, four, or five have to become 10 and 15, and pay has to stay competitive with Southeast Asia. His hope for the industry is 1,000 and then 2,500 people, more customers, and new technology. He says Kaynes is the only true original-design manufacturer in India, and that the group is an electronics manufacturer, an outsourced assembly and test company, and a bare-board circuit-board company.

Key points

  • The plant is Kaynes Semicon in Sanand. The written account names Raghu Panicker as chief executive and Sanjana Gupta as the interviewer. The spoken account addresses Sanjana and does not say Raghu Panicker.
  • The title's 10 billion devices is an intent at full scale, close to 10 billion, not current output. Units are itemized as 1 through 6, and later as six or seven.
  • The site is 46 acres. Customers own the wafer. The line runs from incoming inspection through saw, die attach, wire bond, and tests including ball shear, die shear, and wire pull.
  • A power module is said to hold 17 dice. Unit 2 is 16,000 square metres, under construction, with about 480 to 485 machines and a clean room of about 8,000 square metres.
  • One plating line is running and a second is planned. The chemical is heard as citrine or citron and is said to come from Malaysia for now.
  • Board assembly for communication modules is expected at the end of November. Power is 11 kilovolts now and is to become 66. The water aim is zero liquid discharge.
  • The stated yield standard is 99.999 percent. Automotive quality is also described as having to be 100 percent, because one airbag chip cannot fail. The system is heard as "anti-breaking."
  • The plant is IATF qualified. Later products are for two-wheelers and four-wheelers, then aerospace. Talks have started with the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad.
  • Headcount is 100, with a hope of 500 and 700 in three to four months and then thousands or 2,000. The Government of India has approved 12 companies, and Kaynes is one.
  • Micron and CG Semi are the other plants named in Sanand. He says the three do not compete: memory, microcontrollers, and IPM 5 and IPM 7. He does not assign each product to a company.
  • Floor areas for units 3 through 6 are then added in figures that do not match the storey sizes he stated. Institution names including NMA, Sahasar, and Tanjaw are as heard.

item.title: A Karnataka IT minister calls data centers a necessary evil
item.description:
Asked whether data centres are a very important part of a discussion that is not named, the speaker says they are, and that he does not want to compete with other data centres because that is a race to the bottom. He says he has a responsibility for the environment and a responsibility to see that the next generation gets a better world. Asked whether that is also because the technology is changing so fast, he calls data centres a necessary evil. Speaking as an IT minister, he says he cannot say he does not want them. They are needed. He then asks whether they can be made more effective, whether better power utility effectiveness is there, whether water utility effectiveness is there, and whether newer technology can be adopted. He says that is what he is interested in. The phrases "power utility effectiveness" and "water utility effectiveness" are as heard. The title says data centres are becoming a major political issue. He does not say that. The written account says the necessary evil is for India's digital future and describes a trade-off with rapid expansion and responsible governance. Those phrases are not spoken. The minister is not named.

Key points

  • Speaking as an IT minister, he calls data centres a necessary evil and says he cannot refuse them.
  • He does not want a race to the bottom with other data centres.
  • He cites the environment and the next generation, and he asks for better power utility effectiveness, water utility effectiveness, and newer technology.
  • Those two effectiveness phrases are as heard. No metric is defined.
  • The title's claim that data centres are a major political issue is not said. India is not named in the spoken account. The minister is not named.

item.title: Founders disagree on whether Sarvam stays sovereign while hosting Chinese models
item.description:
Antara asks whether India is building its own AI or becoming a subsidized place to run other companies' models. She says the government is putting billions of dollars into subsidizing tens of thousands of GPUs so startups can build domestic models, and that almost a year after criticism of Sarvam for a model built on top of Mistral, Sarvam's latest move reopened the argument. The written account names her Antara Gupta and lists Siddharth Panwar, chief executive of Mannas, also written NeuroDx, Vishnu Ramesh, co-founder and chief technology officer of Asthra AI, and Vishnu Subramanian, founder of JarvisLabs. The spoken introductions say Antara, Mannas, Asthra AI, and JarvisLabs.ai. Her question assumes that if six of Sarvam's eight token-factory models are Chinese, Sarvam can no longer call itself sovereign. The guests do not state that six-of-eight count.

Vishnu Subramanian says a domestic chip cannot be built in six months, and that sovereignty is not only the model. Inference, training, chips, and the servers that hold the chips all matter, because AI is used in defence, government, and education. On a scale from 0 to 10 he puts India close to one or two, with a possible 10 in 10 or 15 years. He also says more sovereignty could come over 5, 10, or 15 years. Siddharth says that for Mannas's brain work, and for its language models, he does not care where the silicon was made. He compares that to MRI machines India does not make, fighter-jet engines India has not made, and petrol from the Gulf. Gaps have been lived with, and they should be judged by what they do for the country. Vishnu Ramesh says large buyers want the product to work and, in some cases, servers kept in India. For Asthra, working means customers can prepare regulatory documents in four hours instead of 30 to 60 days. In secure and mid-market uses, what customers currently accept is zero data retention: Anthropic and OpenAI attesting that they will not store the usage, let alone train on it.

Vishnu Subramanian calls the Chinese-model question one of positioning. If Sarvam were not serving models, India would consume tokens from outside, and banks and regulated industries cannot take intelligence from beyond the border. He says the best open-weight models in a period he calls "2022 26" come from China, and he asks why American open weights would be acceptable if Chinese ones are treated as a problem. He attributes that objection to Western media. Building India's own open-weight model is a separate job that still has to be done, but as a hosting platform Sarvam may serve the best open models while it builds better ones. Vishnu Ramesh says whether a funded startup favours a foreign model depends on the startup, its board, and its founders. Frontier models are already extremely hard. A model he calls Sarvam 105B may have been slightly competitive when it came out. He has not seen it, and he would have expected it to slip in rankings. He credits Sarvam with showing that a foundation model can come from India, and he says the risk is loss of focus. He has seen smaller companies that raised 2 million or 3 million dollars announce extra products and then return to the original job. A friend he calls Arko, at a company he calls PipeShift, announced retrieval and document parsing after seed funding even though inference was the core, then pivoted back. He hopes Sarvam doubles down on competitive models from India. He rejects stopping because the models cannot match DeepSeek or Google. Voice and Indian languages are an India-specific opening, ElevenLabs is already being paid for that market, and the work needs a narrow focus.

Siddharth says training a foundation model from scratch is not financially irresponsible. Mannas built a compact model that he calls the leading model in the world under 1 billion parameters. Something architecturally new has to start small. A 100-billion-parameter checkpoint will not become a frontier model. He says the government shows decisive intent, Mannas is backed by India, and quitting now would repeat what he calls a "cavary engine," work that would still have to be done 30 years later. That spelling is as heard. Vishnu Subramanian says there is an unhealthy obsession with foundation models. A developer solving one problem should use open-weight tools and reinvent only if those tools fail. A country should keep trying, the way a cricket team keeps entering a World Cup after a loss. Sarvam is taking a shot and Mannas is trying. India was not first to release an OpenAI or Anthropic model. Maybe in 2030 it will be first to a very intelligent model, which requires continued attempts.

Antara says India is scaling to 58,000 subsidized GPUs under the India AI mission, and she asks whether a change in United States export controls would shut the ecosystem down. Vishnu Subramanian calls that hypothetical. He says the subsidized number is unknown, and that Indian companies and foreign clouds such as AWS and Google Cloud own GPUs outside the subsidy. A stop on important hardware would usually come with geopolitical tension and could also hit the computers and phones people use. He says Google, Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, and SpaceX sitting in one country distort the balance of power, and that India needs enough wealth-making companies to be treated fairly when it negotiates. Until then, someone can stop fuel or dictate a price. That cannot be fixed quickly. Vishnu Ramesh says that answer covers the point. Siddharth says the company-level answer is not the country-level one. He says the Strait of Hormuz was blocked and shook the economy, and that if frontier intelligence later feeds every sector and then gets locked, India would be at the mercy of whoever holds it. He still ties sovereignty to Sarvam because it is trying to give India that autonomy. Whether it is a frontier lab can be questioned, because it is not at the top of the leaderboards, but for a defence deployment he says the government would not go to Chinese models or to Mistral. It would ask Sarvam. Vishnu Subramanian says Meta was shipping a promise of the best open weights until Zuckerberg decided that was not in his interest and stopped, and that Chinese companies release open weights for their own reasons. If they stop, users could be told to pay or accept new terms, and India could not then suddenly train a frontier model. Trying and failing is acceptable. A genuine effort matters more than beating Anthropic on a given day. Vishnu Ramesh says it is not a one-week project, and that other initiatives dilute the chance of success. His chief scientist, Professor Manish of IIIT Hyderabad, knows the Sarvam team, holds it in high regard, and sees a strong technical group. Focus is the missing piece. Sarvam has raised a lot of capital, in his account.

On hardware, Vishnu Ramesh says Nvidia dominates because CUDA is the most mature toolkit and most major open-source frameworks for building and fine-tuning models sit largely on it. Asthra's smaller models for document parsing and search, which he calls weak and critical pieces of pharmaceutical document drafting, were built on CUDA. On foreign models and Indian healthcare data, Siddharth says bias is possible, and beyond doubt where judgement is involved. Two doctors with the same training can give different plans. Mannas works with quantitative data, so he says he is more isolated from that, while healthcare overall is a substantial challenge. Vishnu Ramesh says the larger issue for pharmaceutical documents, which can be very valuable intellectual property, is local nuance. A hospital in India and a hospital in the United States operate differently. He is less worried about safety now, because agent harnesses have improved. About a quarter earlier Asthra was building its own harness, then decided that a good harness is itself a major task. They use harnesses he names as Claude Code and Agent SDK, and they focus on model quality and the tools that prepare complex documents. He says an open-source foundation model can be legally acceptable in pharmaceuticals. Customers care that their data benefits only them. Some very large enterprises want a fully sealed deployment with no calls to Anthropic or OpenAI. Asthra can fine-tune a large model for that, and it will not start unless the customer invests or Asthra raises the money. Vishnu Subramanian says this is not his field. As a layman he would be careful: the system is probabilistic, not a fixed answer, and people who do not understand it start treating a prediction as intelligence.

He says open source is not the only path. Proprietary and open technologies have coexisted for 20 or 30-plus years, as with Microsoft and Linux. He expects private labs, maybe Indian frontier models, and open weights from India, China, the United States, or eventually a wider effort. He says training has a dark side. When American companies complain about distillation, Anthropic has paid a penalty for violating copyright in books, and no frontier lab is transparent about its data. A Hugging Face attempt along shared lines did not, in his view, get far, because the money in private models was huge. That could change over several years. Siddharth says hosting foreign models alone would not be sovereignty, but Sarvam has its own models, is preparing better ones, and has a strong team, so he would not take the word away. The frontier label, meaning leading the world, is what can be debated. He says companies receiving government GPU subsidies are required to open their models at this moment, and that he is required to open his brain foundation model, which is open. Vishnu Ramesh says Sarvam broke a barrier and the game is not over. Agents use models at several levels, and new designs are challenging how a language model works. Dilution remains the problem: beyond the open-weight models, Sarvam has announced its own coding agent and some five or six other things.

Vishnu Subramanian says the panel is using a narrow definition. JarvisLabs started so a hobbyist could get a GPU easily. The harder sovereignty problem, he says, is whether any cloud built in India serves the world, while users rely on Amazon, Google, and Microsoft clouds. China could produce open-weight models because its internet was shielded, letting it build its own search, its own ride-hailing, and its own online retail, and thus the wealth and the computers to train. India did not have that shield and started from scratch. On the subsidy, he says the government subsidized a specific Sarvam project, not the entire company, and that Sarvam also has venture funding. From news articles, which he flags as his understanding, they trained on 4,000 GPUs, that project was subsidized, and he hears the project is over. He says they have enough capital and "raised like 300 billion dollars or something," so inference need not run on those subsidized GPUs. The caption says "GPS" once in that sentence. As a private company they may do what they think keeps them alive. He says focus worked for Steve Jobs on his return to Apple, and that other companies succeed by trying many things. Time will show which applies.

Asked whether the public money is real innovation or help for private profit, he says they did not spend billions of taxpayer dollars subsidizing Sarvam, and he puts India itself at 10,000 crore. He says he opened a company called Fluidstack, saw the French president's photo, and saw a claim that 1 million dollars was being put into a large data centre "in French." Compared with some countries, India's spending is limited, and a research project does not have to succeed for the experiment to be legitimate. He rejects a choice between training and inference. Amazon has about a thousand products and JarvisLabs four or five, so the country has to do 10 or 20 times what it does, and Sarvam probably 20 times what it does today. More profitable companies would pay more tax and hire more people. Siddharth agrees with much of that. The grant he knows was a fixed sum for a project. For Mannas that project was the brain foundation model. They delivered it, made it public, and moved on. A one-trillion-parameter model would probably cost 300 million dollars in one shot, which is a different figure from the 300 billion. If that spend is not viable now, Sarvam has to make decisions that keep it alive. He says the government owns 1 to 2 percent of the stock in Sarvam, so the public owns a part. He has found statements suggesting fraud and what is heard as "nonrupless" conduct. As someone inside the system through which Sarvam got the grant, he sees nothing wrong. He points to Mistral and to Macron, who he says made building Mistral a personal mission. Indian decision-making is bureaucratic and accountable in a way private money is not, so some experiments look flawed later. He would not call the past a scandal so much as something to refine. If open models are treated as sovereignty, the government has to plan for the day they stop coming. Vishnu Ramesh says compute for researchers is not enough. Sovereignty, for him, can mean a way to use the technology without depending on one supplier, and open weights already open a lot of that. He has been building document models out of IIIT Hyderabad for seven years, under two startups. India has talent and has not yet had what he calls its space moment in AI. He cites Indian space companies and SpaceX reusable rockets as proof that less money can still produce a result.

Antara says, if she is not wrong, that Siddharth returned from Stanford to build Mannas, while most top researchers stay in Silicon Valley. His reply does not confirm Stanford. He says talent in India matures quickly with computers and permission to be ambitious. In his company, nobody came from abroad with deep experience of language models. They are students he taught. He is faculty at IIT Mandi. Later stages will need outside expertise, and his chief technology officer came from the United States. He says many people he works with have come back. Asked what to do next, Vishnu Subramanian says people should work on what they are curious about. He started JarvisLabs because buying a server in India was very hard, so he had to import one. Vishnu Ramesh says the task is to fill a gap, not to build a foundation model for its own sake. He and his co-founder have seen what he calls Opus 5.5 fall in quality, and he thinks users are being pushed toward more expensive models, which he compares to older phones whose batteries are worn down so people buy again. India will be better prepared if something similar happens at national scale. Siddharth's closing view is that intelligence is a national-security question, and that Mannas exists to challenge the claim that the technology is too hard to build. The closing question, also in the written account, is whether India should build its own chips and foundation models or dominate the application layer. The group does not pick one answer.

Key points

  • Antara asks whether India is building sovereign AI or subsidizing a place to run other companies' models. The written account names her Antara Gupta. The spoken name is Antara.
  • Her premise that six of Sarvam's eight token-factory models are Chinese is not confirmed by the guests. Vishnu Subramanian says regulated firms must host models inside India, and that Sarvam may serve the best open models while it builds its own.
  • He says the best open weights in a period heard as "2022 26" come from China. He scores India's sovereignty near one or two out of ten.
  • Siddharth Panwar of Mannas says he does not care where the silicon comes from for his own models, and that training from scratch is not financially irresponsible. He calls Mannas's compact model the leader under 1 billion parameters.
  • He would keep the word sovereign for Sarvam because it has its own models, and he would argue only about whether it leads the world. For defence, he says the government would ask Sarvam rather than a Chinese model or Mistral.
  • He says the government owns 1 to 2 percent of Sarvam, that subsidy recipients must open their models, and that a one-trillion-parameter model would probably cost 300 million dollars.
  • Vishnu Subramanian's "raised like 300 billion dollars" is a separate, unfinished figure. His 4,000-GPU project, which he says is over, is his reading of news articles.
  • Vishnu Ramesh says Sarvam 105B may have been slightly competitive. He has not seen it. Extra products, including a coding agent and about five or six other things, dilute the work. Professor Manish of IIIT Hyderabad holds the team in high regard.
  • Antara's 58,000 subsidized GPUs are not accepted as a known number. Vishnu Subramanian puts the India figure at 10,000 crore and says billions of taxpayer dollars were not spent subsidizing Sarvam.
  • Asthra prepares regulatory documents in four hours instead of 30 to 60 days, on CUDA, and will fine-tune a sealed model only if the customer or a new round pays for it.
  • Siddharth does not confirm a return from Stanford. He teaches at IIT Mandi. His chief technology officer came from the United States.
  • "Cavary engine," "nonrupless," PipeShift, Arko, and Opus 5.5 are as heard. The panel does not choose between foundation models and the application layer.

item.title: Companies should measure the value of tokens, not the leaderboard
item.description:
Rakesh Ravuri, chief technology officer of Publicis Sapient, the digital consultancy inside Publicis Groupe, says ranking employees by how much artificial intelligence they use was a way to make people try a new tool, not a plan to raise the bill. The introduction says he joined in 2018 from Amazon, where he built the engineering team behind its logistics service. The next words, "ship. Amazon," are unclear. He thanks Sudhi. The written account also calls him senior vice president of engineering and names Sudhi Sachdev. The spoken account says chief technology officer and Sudhi. In April, Meta had a table ranking about 85,000 employees by AI use. First place came with the title token legend, and Meta withdrew the table within the week. Microsoft had run a similar one since January. The introduction calls that a nice initiative and says somewhere a finance director opened the invoice. By July, Publicis Sapient had a name for the habit: tokenmaxxing. A PwC survey of 4,454 chief executives, published in January, found 56 percent saying AI had brought no real significant financial benefit. No year is attached to April, January, July, or February. The question that follows is what a company does after the leaderboard, and whether for some teams the AI now costs more than the people.

Ravuri says people wait for someone else to go first, so a leaderboard runs until use is high enough to ask a different question: how much value the tokens create, and which process actually changed. Incentives are short-lived. He offers a story from the early 1990s that he thinks is in the book The Mythical Man-Month, and he says he might be wrong. A company rewarded people who fixed the most bugs, and people planted bugs so they could fix them. He also says the British in India in the 1800s rewarded whoever caught the most snakes. Hardware sellers, he says, like token counts because the counts sell hardware. Political and social arguments use the same counts to say the work is being done by tokens and people do not matter. Each has some truth. The direction, he says, is still upward, while the predictions fan out. If the tools create value, companies will use more of them and burn more tokens. More use brings more competition, early shortages, then more supply, until the price of a token hits bottom. With open-weight models, a lot of work may run on a local machine.

He compares this with expensive internet lines in the late 1990s, when people said an internet company could not pay the bill, and with the 2008 claim that phone apps would serve only premium users. A fisherman and a farmer now use an app, and he says that market is larger than the web. A phrase heard as "a lion share of our it perspective in India" is unclear. Some companies will be early, some will lag, and some will change, as the internet changed physical retail. Every finance chief should put tokens on the task that creates value fastest and still fund enough trials, as a research budget does, to unlock later value.

The interviewer quotes Alex Karp of Palantir, to CNBC in July: "something has gone completely wrong" with how AI is sold. Ravuri's reply renders the name unclear, as "palent" and "the palenteers car," and he says he sort of agrees that AI is being sold wrong. Many clients use it for efficiency. Having a model write meeting notes may be faster and more accurate, and it adds nothing to the process. His line is that efficiency builds a faster caterpillar, not a butterfly. Putting a skateboard under the old process makes it glide without changing the company. Once every test is automated, a software firm that used AI only to test faster has nothing left. He is taking apart a development cycle used for 30 years and asking which steps are still bottlenecks. He calls the result an AI software development process. The Agile Manifesto, written in 2000, was for people working with people. Humans working with agents, and agents working with agents, need a different one. He created something he calls AI-assisted Agile.

He says a leader should not prescribe the task. Set the aim and let people find the work. He did not mean to skip efficiency. Amazon, for its first 10 years or more, put profits back into the company and was, in his words, an unstoppable force by late 2012. Time that efficiency releases should be used to change the work. His example is software called Slingshot, meant to help build factories in which software builds the software. The team automated the existing process and called the factory done. Releases had moved from every two weeks to once a week. He told them to ship three times a day. They had to take the line apart, ask which steps a three-a-day pace still needs, how to run 10,000 test cases in parallel, and whether a check at one step could be reused. He compares that with a demand that a rocket be reusable, which forces the design to be rethought. He says he grew up around ISRO, saw rockets built, and recalls a rocket engine in the 1980s sent on a bullock cart. His father was in the first batch, 1969 or 1970, that set up ISRO at Sriharikota. An internship design for a fin, he says, evolved into the Chandrayaan rocket, the GSLV Mark III, and he cannot claim much of the credit. The interviewer says he knows the people in that bullock-cart photograph.

Asked how many companies will fund failure, he says the problem is not new. In late 1999 he had to justify a web server the way someone now asks for access to AI. Companies that create efficiencies and reinvest them are the ones that last. AI is the current trigger, not a new kind of company problem. Fast change, he says, is a repeat. In 2008, interface tools changed so quickly that people said nothing meaningful would be built on the web. In 1996, Intel was changing processors every six months or every year. The list he gives is out of order: 486, Pentium, Pentium 2, Pentium 4, Pentium 3, Pentium 4, and Pentium 5. He says there is a constant forgetting. He calls current AI a capable specialist. If he tells his agent what to build, it will build it in 20 minutes. The hard part is knowing what to ask. Creation is also easier. He refers to an example both had seen: four people, given a full specification and a model, created a browser like Chrome in two weeks, against two years by Google's best engineers. A small team of three or four can now do what once needed a large one.

The interviewer cites Bryan Catanzaro of Nvidia, who told Fortune that for his team computing now costs far more than the employees. Ravuri says his first computer in 1996 cost more than his salary, and that a new laptop may cost more than the graduate one hires. The valid point, he says, is that the spending categories change. Around 2007, paying a cloud bill sounded ridiculous because the machines were in the building. He says to compare any company's cloud bill with 10 years ago, setting AI aside. Companies will spend more on AI, and AI will also create more value. What they do with the value depends on the company. They can hire more people because they can attempt more. Roles change. He says that does not mean fewer people, and that each earlier technology increased employment. Bank automation did not leave fewer bank employees. They do different work. There are more carpenters and plumbers than in the 1950s.

The interviewer says the paper described a European bank that cut loan processing from 60 days to six, and asks what changed besides the software. Ravuri answers with the cost of waiting. A 60-day approval can send a good loan to a competitor. The missed revenue is, in his banking terms, the AAA loans the bank could have had. Faster processing lets it serve more of the customers it wanted. The limit was time, not how much money it had to lend. A larger book brings more interest, and six days leaves room for a closer look, for services around the loan, and for collecting bad loans the bank had said it had no time to chase. He asks what to do with the 54 days. It is not about cutting the number of people who process loans. It is about the work those people can now do, including work that had been dismissed as uneconomical. He does not restate the bank's name or the paper citation.

On investors pushing companies that are not ready, he calls it human nature and fear of missing out, larger because the prize looks larger, and present in ordinary conversations, not only among venture firms. The interviewer says Publicis Groupe shares fell about 7 percent in midday trading after full-year results in February, and asks whether that pressure lands inside the consultancy. Ravuri says he does not know which incident is meant. He has not seen a big change in behaviour. People feel energized rather than panicked. Publicis bought Publicis Sapient around 2014 or 2015, before he was there, because media was going to be digital as well as offline. They partnered with Microsoft and created a platform called Marcel around 2016 or 2017, in a phrase heard as "the charad eras." He is not sure of those dates. He says the purpose, stated from an MIT campus in 1992, was to change how companies use technology. The trigger was the internet, then mobile and cloud in the late 2000s, and now AI. He points to public statements by 2018.

Bodhi, which the interviewer describes as a platform sold to other companies for managing AI spend, started in 2019, when the job was to take a machine-learning idea out of a notebook and into production: forecasting, optimization, or a classifier. Generative features were added later. His definition is a platform that helps a company use AI to change a process. Dashboards show the data, who approves a decision, the activity, an audit log, and the spend. AI used to be a capital purchase, machines in a data centre or a fixed cloud bill. It is now a running cost with no natural ceiling, which he compares to a credit card with no limit. Finance chiefs know the shift has to happen and want limits, visibility, and a reconciliation, the way they already do for employee cards. He calls that visibility close to mandatory. The caption breaks off once at "not just meant for giving you," so Bodhi is not only a spend tool, and the rest of that sentence is missing.

Asked what a technology chief should stop doing, he says the T stands for transformation, not technology. Departments will learn to use the tools. His job is to make the use reliable: security, practices where no standard exists yet, and guardrails so it does not fall over or eat the profit. A line then says maturity means he has to stifle another department's creativity, which the interviewer accepts, and the next line says maturity means a safe place to experiment. Those two claims sit next to each other. He says hallucinations have come down, that people ask better questions, and that a model is a probability, set by a top-p or top-k. The interviewer calls him a conductor. Ravuri says there are new instruments, and a garbled line about a trombone is not a clear claim. Few people in the job, he says, have had to introduce a technology, scale it, and replace it, more than once. He has had to do all three.

If a finance chief wants the AI budget cut in half, he says he will find the money by creating value somewhere else, so it does not have to be cut. The interviewer says Salesforce reportedly set a floor of 170 dollars a month in tokens per person. Ravuri says a floor might make sense for one person and should not cap a process that is creating value. He does not confirm the 170 dollars. On an open model from China, GLM 5.2, said to list at about a sixth of the price of GPT 5.5 on its own benchmarks, he says a bank should care because competition will push the price down. He does not confirm the ratio. A router that chooses the model has to be evaluated continuously as models and questions change. Their platform's router is retrained, not trained once and used for five years. The name of that evaluation practice is left unfinished in the account. Told that Gartner expects more than 40 percent of agent projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, he says fail fast is a good pattern. He would cancel a project with no definition of the value it is supposed to create and no way to measure it. An impression is not a result. He does not confirm the 40 percent. Asked whether AI is paying for itself inside Publicis Sapient, he refuses a yes or a no. He calls it a forward-looking statement and says only that it definitely has enough legs.

If token counts become a joke within a year, he expects the next wrong scoreboard to be pride in how many agents a person is running. He calls that agentmaxxing. Within a year or a year and a half, many agents will be working in the background, the way a computer already runs processes the user does not see. Names he gives for those agents are unclear: Grok bots, OpenClaw bots, "her" bots, Muse, "or whatever dots." He says OpenAI and others are already announcing 10,000 agents running in parallel on the Navier-Stokes equation. The useful question is whether the agents are working together. The count, like the token count, can become the thing people boast about.

Key points

  • Rakesh Ravuri, chief technology officer of Publicis Sapient, says token leaderboards were a short adoption push, and the next measure is the value the tokens create.
  • The introduction says Meta ranked about 85,000 employees in April, withdrew a "token legend" title within a week, and that Microsoft had a similar ranking from January. No year is given.
  • A PwC survey of 4,454 chief executives, published in January, found 56 percent reporting no real significant financial benefit from AI.
  • He might be wrong that the bug-leaderboard story is in The Mythical Man-Month. The snake bounty is his second example of a reward that misses the aim.
  • Efficiency, such as model-written meeting notes, is a faster caterpillar, not a new process. He is rebuilding a 30-year software cycle and says the 2000 Agile Manifesto does not cover humans working with agents.
  • A team that had reached one release a week was told to ship three times a day, including 10,000 test cases. The point was to redesign the line.
  • The interviewer says a European bank in the paper cut loans from 60 days to six. Ravuri discusses the 54 days left as time for better loans and collections, not fewer staff. He does not restate the bank.
  • He does not recognise a February drop of about 7 percent in Publicis Groupe shares. The 7 percent, the Salesforce floor of 170 dollars, GLM 5.2 at a sixth of GPT 5.5, and Gartner's 40 percent are the interviewer's figures.
  • Bodhi began in 2019 to put machine learning into production. Spend visibility matters because AI moved from a fixed purchase to a running cost.
  • He will not say AI is paying for itself. He says it has enough legs. A proposed cut of the AI budget in half, he says, can be met by value created elsewhere.
  • He expects a later boast about how many agents are running, which he calls agentmaxxing, within a year or a year and a half. The agent names in that passage are unclear.
  • His father was in the 1969 or 1970 batch at Sriharikota. An internship fin, he says, fed into the GSLV Mark III. He disclaims most of the credit.

item.title: Google's Willow chip won a coordination game 98.3 percent of the time
item.description:
Google's Willow processor won a two-player coordination game on a 3 by 3 grid 98.3 percent of the time. The classical ceiling is 88.9 percent, and the best classical strategy is described as eight wins out of nine. The players do not communicate. Each square is plus one or minus one, every row must multiply to plus one, every column must multiply to minus one, and they win if their answers match where the row and column meet. The hardware did not produce an impossible completed grid. It used quantum measurements to coordinate answers beyond what a pre-arranged classical strategy can achieve. The account presents this as quantum contextuality: the outcomes are not all explained by fixed answers chosen before the compatible measurements. A name heard as Sundar Pay, and later as Pichai, is credited with highlighting contextuality as a possible deeper resource and with calling the result a sharper ruler for building better quantum systems. No full name is spelled out.

The spoken account describes a multiplayer coordination game with up to 71 cubits, and a separate shallow-circuit experiment on up to 105 cubits. The written account says benchmarks on 105 qubits. The stated theoretical advantage is against classical circuits limited in how many sequential steps they can take. Taken together, the experiments are said to show quantum behavior remaining measurable on larger systems, and to expose subtle systematic hardware errors that conventional randomized benchmarks can miss, because tasks that demand precise coordination reveal a pattern a randomized test can hide. The conclusion is that Google has shown a quantum resource at scale that could help diagnose the hardware. Chemistry and material science remain later ambitions, and this result does not deliver them. The account places the result on Thursday.

Key points

  • Willow won a two-player 3 by 3 coordination game 98.3 percent of the time, against a classical ceiling of 88.9 percent.
  • The players do not communicate. Rows must multiply to plus one, columns to minus one, and they win if the answers match where the row and column meet.
  • The best classical strategy is described as eight wins out of nine. The hardware coordinated through quantum measurements and did not produce an impossible grid.
  • The result is tied to quantum contextuality. A name heard as Sundar Pay, and later as Pichai, called it a sharper ruler for building better quantum systems. No full name is spelled out.
  • The spoken account says up to 71 cubits in a multiplayer game and up to 105 cubits in a separate shallow-circuit run. The written account says benchmarks on 105 qubits.
  • The stated advantage is against classical circuits limited in sequential steps. The runs are said to reveal hardware errors that randomized benchmarks can miss.
  • Chemistry and material science are not delivered by this result. The account places it on Thursday.

item.title: Gemini 4 Neon leads a coding-agent index with a score of 58.6
item.description:
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Neon, also spelled Gemini 4 NEON in the written account, for software engineering, analytical work, and tasks that take several steps. It is first on the artificial analysis coding agent index with a score of 58.6. That combined score is more specific than a claim that Neon beats every competing model at coding. The index mixes understanding a codebase, changing code, fixing a bug, and command-line work. A model can do well on one kind and struggle on another, and the testing organization advises reading the combined score beside the individual results. Google's published comparison shows Neon ahead on some evaluations, while Claude Opus 5.5 remains ahead on others, including Terminal Bench 4.1 and Frontier Code 2.0. Understanding an unfamiliar repository and repairing it ask different things of an agent.

Neon supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens. Google lists documents, images, audio, and video among the inputs. The model offers four thinking levels that control how much reasoning it applies. API pricing is 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 dollars per million output tokens, with a lower rate for cached input and no figure for that lower rate. Those are usage rates. The bill for a job depends on tokens consumed, including extra attempts. Google is rolling Neon out through its developer and business services, with access for eligible paid users in a service named anti-gravity and in the Gemini app. Testing it on the work a team actually does will say more than one ranking.

Key points

  • Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon for software engineering, analysis, and multi-step tasks. The written spelling is Gemini 4 NEON.

item.title: Karnataka promises five lakh Nipuna jobs as fresher IT hiring falls
item.description:
At the Bengaluru Tech Summit, Sudhi Sachdev spoke with Priyank Kharge. The listing identifies Kharge as Karnataka's ITBT and RDPR minister. The conversation introduces him as minister for Home, ITBT and e-commerce. Sachdev's summit figures were more than 10,000 delegates over three days, more than 700 speakers, 1,500 exhibitors, 65 countries, and 1,000 startups from 100 cities. Kharge said 75 countries are represented. Sachdev said Elevate is in its tenth year and that 1,500 startups have been funded, and he called this the 29th edition. Kharge said some of the state's best policies came from the summit, and that frontier technologies mean government has to listen or be left behind. The state has roundtables on sustainable data centers, AI in agriculture and aerospace, marine biotech, bioengineering, and AI for biogenetics, including responsible AI.

Kharge described a government-first policy. A startup whose innovation helps the government gets 25 lakh rupees and a pilot in a regulatory sandbox, and the state scales it if the pilot succeeds, so government becomes the first customer. He said the state wants to go further, especially in deep tech, and is ready to take up a drought-proof or disease-proof seed, seaweed for commercial extraction, early cancer detection, and better rural citizen services. Those are examples of appetite, not completed rollouts. Sachdev's figures, not Kharge's, were that Bengaluru accounts for nearly a third of India's AI investment, 85 billion dollars in startup funding, and 57 unicorns valued at 211 billion dollars. He also cited a think-tank ranking of India at 11th of 56 countries on AI readiness, and said 60.5 percent of Indians aged 15 to 29 had a mobile phone.

Kharge said AI readiness is both skill and infrastructure, and that India is number five in the world in skill. He called Nipuna Karnataka India's biggest reskilling programme, said five lakh jobs are promised, and said training has already started for close to 63,000 people in modules including Gemini, OpenAI, and Claude. GCCs and the service sector set the courses. The state scales them. He is not prescribing one subject. He pointed to biology, agriculture, including an MSE in agriculture, and using biology and AI to raise yields where cultivable land is limited. Sachdev cited a staffing firm he called iso: fresher IT hiring fell from 6 lakh in fiscal 2022 to about 1.2 lakh in fiscal 2025, and he said Kharge had called the disruption brief last August. Kharge said brief can be a year or a couple of years, compared it with COVID, and said the answer is to upskill inside one's own field.

On data centers, Kharge said he needs them and called them a necessary evil, but he will not race other states to the bottom. He wants them sustainable, with better power and water effectiveness. He said no state has a sustainable data-center policy and that this is what Karnataka is about. He did not describe a published policy as already in force. Data centers create some jobs, not at service-sector scale. On a 2024 local-hiring bill, Sachdev described 50 percent of management jobs and 70 percent of non-management private jobs for locals, and said it was paused over industry resistance. Kharge said it is not resistance. Kannadigas have to be skilled locals. He said people skilled in Bengaluru work in Boston, London, New York, and Melbourne. A gray area remains, some cases are pending in the High Court, and he said skills will decide it.

  • Kharge wants sustainable data centers and said no state has a sustainable data-center policy. He did not say a published policy is already in force.

item.title: Anthropic's share sale is about 81.3 billion dollars at 83 dollars a share

item.title: Modi asks industry to plan for 20 years and build imported inputs in India
item.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke at FICCI's annual general meeting and convention at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 19 November. As FICCI enters its centenary year, he asked companies to plan for the next two decades and to treat India as the basis for long-term investment. The wording of that second phrase was unclear. He pointed to medicines India exports while it still imports ingredients, including active pharmaceutical ingredients, bulk drugs, and intermediates; to iron ore exported while steel products are imported; and to substantial reserves, in a word heard unclearly as boxite, while specialised aluminium alloys come from abroad. He asked which of those capabilities can be built at home. A factory, he said, needs a repeatable process at a competitive cost, not only a design. He pointed to India's small share of global hand-tool and power-tool exports and asked larger firms to help smaller manufacturers. He also named packaging equipment, irrigation systems, and factory machinery for developing countries. The address did not announce a new AI programme or a semiconductor programme.

item.title: Karnataka's centers employ about 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals
item.description:
A report from Zenov and the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission says Karnataka has 1,088 global capability centers, 51 percent of India's total, and more than 120 dedicated AI and machine learning centers of excellence across more than 100 of those centers. Those centers account for nearly half of the country's AI centers of excellence in this corporate ecosystem. Roughly one in three has a mandate covering generative or agentic AI. The work spans software development, chip design, financial operations, healthcare, and predictive maintenance. Karnataka's centers employ around 111,000 AI and machine learning professionals, 43 percent of the national talent pool in those fields inside global capability centers. item.title: Target opens an 830,000 square foot Bengaluru campus for 5,700 employees
item.description:
Antara Gupta speaks with Natarajan Ramamurthy, vice president of data engineering at Target in India, and Ashutosh Bisht, head of research and advisory at AIM, after Target opened an 830,000 square foot Bengaluru campus for 5,700 employees. Ramamurthy says India and Minneapolis are run as one headquarters. Some new-store design is led from India, and most of his data analytics functions are led from India, with US teams still contributing. A Bengaluru team can ship a guest-experience fix through the same checks used in both countries. He says inventory is hard to keep accurate across about 2,000 US stores, online sales, and distribution centers. Real-time signals matter for Target.com and are not worth the cost, in his view, for slow own-brand development. He estimates that about 20 to 30 percent of capacity keeps systems running and close to 70 percent goes to new guest features. Around Thanksgiving, changes stay small and are rolled out in stages. Humans can override an AI decision, those overrides are kept to improve the model, and a person remains the failsafe. Generative AI is not banned in data pipelines by a fixed rule. Staff are meant to understand US stores through onboarding, augmented and virtual walkthroughs, a guest-experience center, and visits. He looks for curiosity, software fundamentals, systems thinking, and retail domain knowledge, and he will not name one shopper-visible change a year ahead.

Bisht says India has more than 2,100 of these centers, about 2.6 million people in them, about 600,000 to 700,000 in retail, and a revenue contribution he puts at almost 100 billion. He puts retail centers at about 70 to 80, or about 170 to 180 including fast-moving consumer goods, and names Target, Lowe's, and Walmart as mature examples. He says only about 20 percent of their AI pilots reach production, with retail around 22 to 25 percent in AIM roundtables. About 9 to 10 percent of the retail-center workforce is in AI, only about 2 percent of that group has eight or more years of experience, and about half to 60 percent of recent AI hires in retail centers came from outside retail. He says Lowe's Mylo product, built with OpenAI, was developed in the Indian unit. He says only about 500 Forbes 2000 companies have an India center, and that more than 350 further US companies could still open one. These are the speakers' figures.

Key points

item.title: OpenAI reports up to 14 percent circuit gains on AMD GPUs in under five months
item.description:
OpenAI says its models found up to 14 percent improvements in power, performance, and area on flagship AMD GPU circuitry that AMD engineers had already spent years optimizing. OpenAI describes that as roughly a year's progress in less than five months. The same account says this does not mean the finished GPU is 14 percent faster. The models worked on the circuit description engineers write. Tools the report names as Synopsis checked that a rewrite still behaved as the original circuit. According to OpenAI, AMD also verified a single-digit percentage gain in power and performance across key blocks of an upcoming flagship CPU. Greg Brockman said some results are in a design recently finalized for manufacturing, and that other improvements are in AMD's production design files for future versions. How those AMD changes perform in physical chips is still open. Separately, on a chip the report calls Alapino and describes as OpenAI's first custom inference chip, a model-proposed multiplier redesign used about 15 percent less cell area and cut latency from two clock cycles to one. OpenAI estimates about a 10 percent reduction in standard cell area in that project's matrix unit, checked when the manufactured chip was powered on.

Key points

  • OpenAI says the AMD work produced up to 14 percent gains in power, performance, and area on flagship GPU circuitry.
  • OpenAI describes that as about a year's progress in less than five months.
  • The account says the finished GPU is not thereby 14 percent faster.
  • Tools named as Synopsis checked that rewritten circuits still behaved as before.
  • OpenAI says AMD verified a single-digit percentage power and performance gain on key blocks of an upcoming flagship CPU.
  • Greg Brockman said some results are in a design finalized for manufacturing, and others are in files for future versions.
  • Performance of the AMD changes in physical chips is still open.
  • On a chip called Alapino, a multiplier redesign used about 15 percent less cell area and one clock cycle instead of two, and the matrix unit's standard cell area fell about 10 percent.

item.title: Experity's chief technology officer describes AI scribes and billing agents for urgent care
item.description:
Saji Rajasekharan, chief technology officer of Experity, says the company's clearest AI gains in urgent care are in coding and billing: fewer denials, faster payment, and more accurate coding. An AI scribe listens to the assessment and the diagnosis and writes structured notes into the medical record. He says clinicians often spend two or three hours or more a day finishing notes, including at home. Care Agent lets a patient look for care in a chat without another password and sends the reason for the visit into the record. Experity requires the provider to review and sign off. He describes about 80 to 100 patients a day in flu season and about 25 off season. He says one client's discharge instructions cut call volume and shortened the closing conversation from about 15 minutes to about 2 minutes. He puts the scale at about 7,000 clinics and 40 million patients. Experity acquired Exdion a few months ago, an AI product covering the path from a closed chart to payment, and he is using that team to grow engineers in Bengaluru who own products for American urgent care. He says the company believes it is already the operating system for urgent care among the top 20 US enterprise operators. Autonomous clinical decisions are a later step. He referred to a Karnataka reskilling scheme he believes is called Nipuna.

item.title: SmartFab, Cyber Evolution, and Unitree's India partner look for work at the summit

A Cyber Evolution representative based in Yelahanka says the Italian network-detection product has been in production for five and a half years and is meant to stop a threat before it becomes an incident. item.title: Kris Gopalakrishnan expects AI to expand work for Indian IT services
item.description:
Kanishk Singh speaks with Kris Gopalakrishnan, co-founder of Infosys and chairman of Axilor Ventures, on day two of the Bengaluru Tech Summit. Gopalakrishnan says every institution has to teach students to use AI tools. Four agreements signed at the summit, including with Google, are meant to train about two lakh people. IIIT Bangalore's AI hub will train trainers and retrain people already in IT. The university's own degree and research programs are probably a year or two away, not the next academic year. Shorter programs, including ones Keonics is starting, can begin sooner. He says agentic AI in public services is inevitable, and the responsible AI committee's first job is to keep that use safe and private. He referred to an announcement from the day before, a name he only roughly recalled, for a data space in which the data stays put and only the changed weights leave. Asked about a figure of about 60,000 GPUs at 18 percent utilization, he says startups still find access difficult and expensive, and he wants capacity spread out rather than held in one place. He points to analog-computing research he works on at the Indian Institute of Science as a possible route to cheaper matrix computation if it is developed further.

He expects AI to expand IT services work, because new tools still have to be joined to older systems and existing data has to be prepared. Programming might fall from about 10 percent of a project to 1 or 2 percent, but he does not expect a significant long-term cut in the workload. He cites growth from 115 million dollars in 1993 to 300 billion dollars and says sector employment, including chip design, will keep rising. Asked about a 15 percent decline in the Nifty this year, he says investors chase the fastest returns, and that five or seven companies are about 40 percent of US market value. Every IT employee has to be retrained, and students finishing now will need extra training. Axilor is a closed fund with four or five general partners. It is shifting toward deep tech without becoming deep-tech only, and it starts two or three companies a year. He describes a government research fund as one lakh crore. He puts the summit at about 21,000 visitors the day before, with an expectation of 60,000 to one lakh, 750 speakers, and 1,500 exhibits.

item.title: Qbit Force claims about 40 crore rupees in revenue without venture capital
item.description:
Sanjana Gupta speaks with L. Venkata Subramaniam, founder and chief executive of Qbit Force. He says the first two systems, one with 5 qubits and one with 25 qubits, go down to milli-Kelvin temperatures, and the conversation tied those systems to Amaravati. Q-Shiva is a lower-cost system so colleges can test hardware. The in-house Nada processor is gold-plated, its packaging was done in Machilipatnam, and he says it holds niobium resonators for about five qubits at frequencies such as 5, 5.5, and 6 gigahertz. Niobium is superconducting around 8 Kelvin, so those resonators can be tested without a dilution refrigerator, while the qubits themselves need milli-Kelvin temperatures. Helium-4 could replace helium-3 if the operating temperature rises. He says helium-3 is not found naturally on Earth. He credits Professor Premalatha with teaching AI at PES College in Mandya in 1991. A 16-year-old girl who was shown the open cooling system later filed a patent on it. The company, started last December, is about to export systems to research labs. He turned down term sheets that would have given an investor control over hiring and markets, and he and a co-founder used their own money, including retirement funds. He names SRM, Qubitech, Chandigarh University, and BIBS as supporters placing orders, and he claims about 40 crore rupees in revenue within the first year. He says he met minister Ajay Singh. No priority export country is named.

Key points

  • L. Venkata Subramaniam says Qbit Force's first systems have 5 and 25 qubits and were discussed in connection with Amaravati.
  • Q-Shiva is for colleges to test hardware. The Nada processor's packaging was done in Machilipatnam.

item.title: Neysa brings 8,192 AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs online in Mumbai
